items.q: A 24-year-old athlete undergoes arthroscopic anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) reconstruction. Postoperatively, the knee achieves full terminal extension readily, but there is persistent stiffness with an inability to flex beyond 70 degrees. Intraoperative review reveals that the graft overtightens as the knee is brought into flexion. Which technical error during tunnel preparation is the most likely cause?
o: Femoral tunnel placed too low on the lateral notch wall
items.e: The most common technical error in ACL reconstruction is placing the femoral tunnel too anteriorly. An anteriorly positioned femoral tunnel increases the distance between tunnel apertures during flexion, causing the graft to tighten excessively in flexion, which leads to loss of flexion or premature graft failure and stretching.
items.note: Accurate, well-constructed clinical question testing the classic and most common technical error in ACL reconstruction.

items.q: Regarding the functional anatomy and bundle biomechanics of the posterior cruciate ligament (PCL), which of the following statements is correct?
o: The anterolateral bundle is the larger bundle and tightens in knee flexion
The posteromedial bundle is larger than the anterolateral bundle and tightens in knee flexion
The ligament of Humphrey originates from the lateral meniscus and courses posterior to the PCL
The PCL is approximately half as strong and narrower than the anterior cruciate ligament
items.e: The PCL consists of two main bundles: the anterolateral (AL) bundle, which is larger and tightens in flexion, and the posteromedial (PM) bundle, which tightens in extension. The PCL is twice as strong and wider than the ACL. The meniscofemoral ligament of Humphrey runs anterior to the PCL, whereas Wrisberg runs posterior.
items.note: Standard high-yield anatomical and biomechanical facts directly aligned with reference authority.

items.q: A 30-year-old male is evaluated following a sports-related knee injury. Physical examination demonstrates an increase of 15 degrees of external rotation compared to the contralateral uninjured knee at 30 degrees of knee flexion. However, when the dial test is performed at 90 degrees of knee flexion, external rotation is symmetrical between both knees. Which structure has been injured?
o: Combined anterior cruciate ligament and medial collateral ligament
Combined posterior cruciate ligament and posterolateral corner
items.e: The dial test evaluates external rotational laxity. An increase in external rotation greater than 10 degrees at 30 degrees of flexion only denotes an isolated posterolateral corner (PLC) injury. Increased external rotation at both 30 and 90 degrees of flexion indicates a combined PCL and PLC injury.
items.note: Classic diagnostic criterion for knee ligament evaluation; unambiguous and perfectly matches reference guidelines.

items.q: Which of the following radiographic findings is considered pathognomonic of an anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) tear?
o: Avulsion fracture of the fibular styloid (Arcuate sign)
Cortical avulsion fracture of the anterolateral tibial plateau (Segond fracture)
Deep sulcus terminalis measuring over 1.5 mm on the medial femoral condyle
Avulsion fracture of the anterior tibial tuberosity
items.e: A Segond fracture represents an avulsion fracture of the lateral capsular margin (anterolateral ligament/capsule) at the anterolateral tibial plateau and is pathognomonic of an ACL tear. The arcuate sign represents a fibular styloid avulsion characteristic of posterolateral corner injury.
items.note: Factually sound, unambiguous, and core superspeciality knowledge.

items.q: An 11-year-old boy presents following a fall from his bicycle with acute right knee haemarthrosis. Plain radiographs demonstrate a displaced type II tibial spine (eminence) fracture. Closed reduction in full extension under conscious sedation is attempted but fails to achieve anatomical reduction. Which anatomical structure is most commonly entrapped at the fracture site blocking closed reduction?
o: Posterior horn of the lateral meniscus
Intermeniscal ligament or anterior horn of the medial meniscus
items.e: In displaced or irreducible Meyers and McKeever type II and III tibial spine (eminence) fractures, closed reduction is most frequently blocked by soft-tissue entrapment of either the anterior horn of the medial meniscus or the transverse intermeniscal ligament.
items.note: Classic paediatric sports orthopaedic fact referenced directly in Campbell's.

items.q: Regarding graft biomechanics and biological incorporation in anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction, which of the following is correct?
o: Quadrupled hamstring tendon autografts demonstrate an ultimate load to failure of approximately 4,000 N
Bone-patellar tendon-bone autografts incorporate primarily by soft-tissue-to-bone healing over 8 to 12 weeks
The reconstructed graft is biomechanically at its weakest point at 1 to 2 weeks postoperatively
A hamstring autograft diameter of less than 10 mm is associated with significantly higher failure rates
items.e: Quadrupled hamstring tendon autografts are the strongest ACL graft option with an ultimate tensile load of approximately 4,000 N (compared to ~2,900 N for BPTB). BPTB incorporates via bone-to-bone healing in 6-8 weeks. During biological ligamentisation, grafts are at their weakest at about 6-12 weeks. Hamstring autografts under 8 mm in diameter correlate with increased failure rates.
items.note: Well-differentiated options with precise biomechanical and incorporation data.

items.q: During transtibial posterior cruciate ligament (PCL) reconstruction, the popliteal artery is at risk of direct penetration during tibial tunnel drilling. Which technical measure is recommended to maximise the safety margin and protect the neurovascular bundle?
o: Maintain the knee in full terminal extension
Keep the knee flexed at 90 degrees
Apply an extreme varus stress during drilling
Avoid using a posteromedial safety portal
items.e: During transtibial PCL tunnel reaming, the popliteal artery lies immediately posterior to the posterior capsule. Keeping the knee flexed at 90 degrees allows the neurovascular structures to fall posteriorly away from the joint capsule and tibial insertion, significantly reducing the risk of vascular penetration, especially when combined with a retractor via a posteromedial portal.
items.note: Vital surgical technique and safety question for superspeciality arthroscopy.

items.q: A 34-year-old male sustains a high-energy dashboard injury during a road traffic accident. Magnetic resonance imaging reveals complete tears of the anterior cruciate ligament, posterior cruciate ligament, and the posterolateral corner structures, with an intact medial collateral ligament. According to the Schenck classification system, this multiligament knee injury is classified as:
items.e: Under the Schenck classification of knee dislocations and multiligament knee injuries: KD I involves a single cruciate tear with collateral injury; KD II involves both cruciates (ACL + PCL) with intact collaterals; KD III involves both cruciates with one collateral complex torn (KD III M for MCL involvement, and KD III L for PLC/lateral involvement); KD IV involves tears of all four major ligament structures (ACL, PCL, MCL, and PLC).
items.note: Standard classification question for multiligament knee injuries.

items.q: The extracellular matrix of the human meniscus consists predominantly of type I collagen arranged in distinct structural orientations. Which fibres are primarily responsible for resisting longitudinal splitting of the meniscal tissue?
items.e: In meniscal fibrocartilage, radial ("tie") fibres interlace between dominant circumferential fibres to resist longitudinal splitting, while circumferential fibres withstand axial loads by converting them into hoop stresses.
items.note: Accurate, well-constructed question matching Campbell's biomechanics of meniscal collagen ultrastructure.

items.q: A 54-year-old woman experiences a sudden painful "pop" in the posterior medial knee while rising from a deep squat. MRI reveals a radial tear 7 mm from the tibial insertion of the posterior horn of the medial meniscus, along with 4 mm of medial meniscal extrusion. Which statement regarding this injury is correct?
o: Circumferential hoop stress dissipation remains preserved due to an intact peripheral rim
It is biomechanically and functionally equivalent to a total meniscectomy
Arthroscopic partial meniscectomy is the established definitive standard of care
It carries minimal risk of subsequent subchondral insufficiency fracture
items.e: A meniscal root tear (occurring within 1 cm of the tibial attachment) disrupts circumferential continuity, leading to loss of hoop stress transmission and meniscal extrusion (>3 mm), making it functionally equivalent to a total meniscectomy.
items.note: Directly supported clinical vignette reflecting modern meniscal root kinematics and pathology.

items.q: A 9-year-old child presents with a painless, palpable clunk and "snapping knee syndrome" on terminal extension. Arthroscopy demonstrates a discoid lateral meniscus that lacks its posterior meniscotibial (coronary) ligament attachment and is anchored posteriorly solely by the meniscofemoral ligament. Under the Watanabe classification, this is categorized as:
items.e: Watanabe Type III (Wrisberg variant) discoid meniscus lacks normal posterior coronary/meniscotibial attachments and retains only the meniscofemoral ligament of Wrisberg, resulting in hypermobility and classic snapping knee syndrome.
items.note: Classic pediatric arthroscopy knowledge accurately tested.

items.q: During an inside-out repair of an unstable tear involving the posterior horn and body of the lateral meniscus, which surgical interval is developed to safely protect the peroneal nerve?
o: Retract the biceps femoris tendon anteriorly and dissect posterior to the lateral gastrocnemius
Retract the iliotibial band posteriorly and dissect anterior to the popliteus tendon
Retract the lateral gastrocnemius anteriorly and dissect posterior to the plantaris muscle
Retract the biceps femoris tendon posteriorly and dissect anterior to the lateral head of gastrocnemius
items.e: In the posterolateral approach for inside-out meniscal repair, the peroneal nerve is protected by retracting the biceps femoris tendon posteriorly and working anterior to the lateral head of the gastrocnemius to place a protective retractor against the capsule.
items.note: Standard surgical anatomy and technique tested in superspeciality arthroscopy exams.

items.q: In normal articular hyaline cartilage, which architectural zone has the highest concentration of proteoglycans and the lowest water content?
items.e: The deep (radial) zone has collagen fibres arranged perpendicular to the joint surface and contains the highest proteoglycan concentration and lowest water content, providing resistance against compressive loads.
items.note: Textbook zonal cartilage histology and biochemistry question.

items.q: When comparing the biochemical alterations of normal articular cartilage ageing with those seen in early osteoarthritis, which of the following is characteristic of early osteoarthritis?
items.e: In early osteoarthritis, keratan sulphate decreases, chondroitin sulphate increases, and water content increases due to a damaged collagen network. In contrast, normal ageing is marked by decreased water content and increased keratan sulphate.
items.note: High-yield differentiation between cartilage ageing and osteoarthritis biochemistry.

items.q: In first-generation autologous chondrocyte implantation (ACI) where cultured chondrocytes were placed beneath an autologous periosteal cover, which of the following was the most frequent graft-specific complication?
items.e: Periosteal patch hypertrophy was the most common complication of first-generation ACI, often requiring secondary arthroscopic debridement and prompting the transition to collagen membranes and matrix-seeded scaffolds (MACI).
items.note: Standard history and complications of cartilage restoration techniques.

items.q: A 15-year-old athlete with persistent knee pain has a suspected osteochondritis dissecans (OCD) lesion on the lateral aspect of the medial femoral condyle. On MRI, which feature indicates instability of the OCD fragment?
o: Homogeneous low T1 signal without a demarcation zone
Intact overlying articular cartilage without subchondral breach
Absence of cystic change in the adjacent subchondral bed
High T2 signal line surrounding the osteochondral fragment
items.e: A high T2 signal line rimming the back of the fragment indicates synovial fluid tracking behind the lesion, which is an established MRI sign of osteochondritis dissecans instability.
items.note: Established MRI diagnostic criteria for osteochondritis dissecans instability.

items.q: A lateral radiograph of a 19-year-old female with recurrent patellar dislocation demonstrates a crossing sign along with a double contour line representing a hypoplastic medial facet, but no supratrochlear spur. According to the Dejour classification, this trochlear dysplasia is classified as:
items.e: Dejour Type C trochlear dysplasia is defined by the presence of a crossing sign together with a double contour line (reflecting a hypoplastic medial facet and convex lateral facet). Type B features a crossing sign with a supratrochlear spur, while Type D combines the crossing sign, spur, and double contour to form a 'cliff' pattern.
items.note: Accurate classic classification question with clear, non-overlapping criteria directly supported by standard literature.

items.q: A 22-year-old male undergoes MPFL reconstruction for recurrent lateral patellar instability. Postoperatively, he has persistent medial patellofemoral pain and significant restriction of knee flexion beyond 90 degrees. Intraoperative fluoroscopy review is most likely to show which femoral tunnel error?
o: Placement too distal to Schöttle point
Placement too proximal to Schöttle point
Placement too anterior to the posterior cortex line
Placement precisely at the adductor tubercle
items.e: In MPFL reconstruction, a femoral tunnel placed too proximal to the anatomical Schöttle point causes the graft to tighten abnormally as the knee flexes. This error leads to loss of flexion and medial patellofemoral joint overload. A tunnel placed too distal results in a graft that is tight in extension and loose in flexion.
items.note: High-yield surgical biomechanics pearl commonly tested in superspeciality exams; fully supported by Campbell's.

items.q: During knee range of motion, at which degree of flexion does the odd facet of the patella make contact with the medial femoral condyle?
items.e: The patella engages the trochlea at 20-30 degrees of flexion at its distal pole and contact moves proximally as flexion increases. The contact area reaches its maximum at 90 degrees, whereas the odd facet contacts the medial femoral condyle only in deep flexion at 120-135 degrees.
items.note: Classic anatomical/biomechanical question directly verified against standard orthopaedic texts.

items.q: A 28-year-old woman presents with recurrent patellar instability and anterior knee pain. Her TT-TG distance on CT is 22 mm. Diagnostic arthroscopy reveals a focal full-thickness chondral defect. Anteromedialisation tibial tubercle osteotomy (Fulkerson) is CONTRAINDICATED if the chondral lesion is located at which site?
items.e: Anteromedialisation of the tibial tubercle unloads the distal and lateral facets of the patella by anteriorising and medialising the extensor mechanism. However, this shifts contact pressures onto the proximal and medial patellar facets, making proximal or medial facet chondral lesions a direct contraindication.
items.note: Crucial surgical decision-making pearl regarding the biomechanics of Fulkerson AMZ osteotomy.

items.q: According to the Dejour criteria for patellofemoral instability, which of the following parameters is considered an abnormal threshold defining a major instability factor?
o: Tibial tubercle-trochlear groove (TT-TG) distance greater than 20 mm
Patellar tilt less than 10 degrees on CT
items.e: The four Dejour major instability factors are trochlear dysplasia, patella alta, patellar tilt over 20 degrees, and an increased TT-TG distance over 20 mm. An Insall-Salvati ratio below 0.8 or Caton-Deschamps index below 0.6 denotes patella baja rather than alta.
items.note: Tests exact diagnostic cut-offs defining major surgical risk factors in patellofemoral instability.

items.q: A 13-year-old male football player with open distal femoral and proximal tibial physes sustains a recurrent lateral patellar dislocation with a TT-TG distance of 21 mm. Which of the following surgical procedures is strictly CONTRAINDICATED in this patient?
items.e: Bony tibial tubercle osteotomy is contraindicated in skeletally immature patients with open physes due to the high risk of anterior proximal tibial epiphysiodesis leading to a genu recurvatum deformity. Soft-tissue procedures such as the Roux-Goldthwait procedure are used when distal realignment is needed in children.
items.note: Standard paediatric sports medicine contraindication.

items.q: Following an acute first-time lateral patellar dislocation, osteochondral fractures occur in approximately 25–50% of knees. Which site is most commonly involved?
items.e: Osteochondral fractures accompany 25-50% of acute patellar dislocations. The most frequent site is the inferomedial patellar facet, caused by impact against the lateral femoral condyle during relocation, followed by the lateral femoral condyle itself.
items.note: High-yield injury pattern question with unambiguous factual backing in Campbell's.

items.q: A 24-year-old woman underwent an isolated lateral retinacular release for patellar instability at an outside clinic. She now presents with disabling anterior knee pain and a subjective sensation of giving way. Examination reveals excessive medial patellar translation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.e: Isolated lateral retinacular release is not indicated for patellofemoral instability and can result in iatrogenic medial patellar instability, particularly when the vastus lateralis tendon is excessively detached. Management requires repair or reconstruction of the lateral retinaculum.
items.note: Recognised post-surgical complication emphasizing why isolated lateral release is abandoned for patellar instability.

items.q: In the glenohumeral joint, which ligament acts as the primary static restraint against anterior translation when the arm is positioned in approximately 45 degrees of abduction and external rotation?
o: Posterior band of the inferior glenohumeral ligament
items.e: The middle glenohumeral ligament (MGHL) provides the primary restraint to anterior translation at approximately 45 degrees of abduction with external rotation. In contrast, the anterior band of the IGHL is the primary restraint at 90 degrees of abduction and external rotation, while the SGHL resists inferior translation in adduction.
items.note: Accurate, standard orthopaedic anatomy question matching source notes.

items.q: An 18-year-old woman presents with recurrent, non-traumatic shoulder subluxations. Physical examination and electromyography demonstrate dyssynchronous, involuntary muscle recruitment causing humeral head displacement without any structural labral or capsular tear. According to the Stanmore triangle classification, what is the polar category and the recommended management?
o: Polar III; arthroscopic rotator interval closure
items.e: Polar III in the Stanmore triangle denotes non-structural, muscle-patterning instability characterised by abnormal muscle recruitment. Management is strictly non-operative, focusing on physiotherapy and biofeedback, while surgery must be avoided because of high failure and complication rates.
items.note: Directly supported by the reference notes and standard shoulder instability classifications.

items.q: During the Latarjet procedure, the coracoid process with the conjoint tendon is transferred to the anteroinferior glenoid rim. According to Patte's 'triple blocking effect', which mechanism provides the primary stability when the arm is in the vulnerable position of abduction and external rotation?
o: Extension of the articular arc by the coracoid bone block
Repair of the native capsule to the coracoacromial ligament stump
Rigid compression of the subscapularis tendon by bicortical screws
Dynamic sling effect of the conjoint tendon on the lower subscapularis
items.e: The triple blocking effect comprises the bony effect, the sling effect, and the capsular repair. In the provocative position of abduction and external rotation, the dynamic sling effect of the conjoint tendon pressing across the lower subscapularis and anteroinferior capsule is the most important stabilizing factor.
items.note: Accurate description of Patte's biomechanical analysis of the Latarjet procedure.

items.q: A 22-year-old collegiate athlete has recurrent anterior shoulder instability. Preoperative 3D CT demonstrates 12% anteroinferior glenoid bone loss. The Hill-Sachs interval measures 24 mm, and the glenoid track width is calculated as 20 mm. According to the Di Giacomo treatment algorithm, what is the most appropriate surgical management?
o: Arthroscopic Bankart repair combined with remplissage
Latarjet coracoid transfer combined with humeral head allograft
items.e: Because the glenoid bone loss is under 25% (subcritical) but the Hill-Sachs interval exceeds the glenoid track width (24 mm > 20 mm), the lesion is classified as 'off-track' (engaging). The algorithm dictates an arthroscopic Bankart repair combined with a remplissage procedure to convert the intra-articular humeral defect to an extra-articular one.
items.note: Classic glenoid track calculation and management problem following standard algorithms.

items.q: A 38-year-old man presents following an electric shock with shoulder pain and an arm locked in internal rotation. Radiographs and CT reveal a posterior glenohumeral dislocation with an impaction fracture of the anteromedial humeral head involving 35% of the articular surface. What is the definitive procedure of choice?
o: Closed reduction and sling immobilisation in internal rotation
McLaughlin procedure (transfer of subscapularis into the defect)
items.e: For a reverse Hill-Sachs (McLaughlin) defect involving 25% to 50% of the anteromedial humeral head following posterior dislocation, the treatment of choice is the McLaughlin procedure (transfer of the subscapularis tendon into the defect) or its Neer modification (lesser tuberosity transfer). Defects under 25% can be treated closed, while those over 50% typically require arthroplasty.
items.note: Standard threshold-based question matching Campbell's guidelines for posterior dislocation defects.

items.q: On coronal oblique MRI of a patient with recurrent post-traumatic shoulder instability, avulsion of the inferior glenohumeral ligament complex from its humeral insertion results in a retracted, downward-curving ligament. This characteristic radiological finding is termed the:
items.e: Humeral avulsion of the glenohumeral ligament (HAGL) represents detachment of the IGHL from the anatomic neck of the humerus. On coronal MRI, the normally U-shaped inferior capsular pouch falls inferiorly, forming a pathognomonic 'J sign'.
items.note: Directly supported by the notes; tests a classic MRI sign in shoulder arthroscopy.

items.q: In the Instability Severity Index Score (ISIS) described by Balg and Boileau to predict recurrence after arthroscopic Bankart repair, which of the following variables is assigned 1 point?
o: Loss of anteroinferior glenoid contour on AP radiograph
items.e: In the ISIS system, shoulder hyperlaxity (external rotation > 85° or Gagey test > 90°) and contact/overhead sports are assigned 1 point each. In contrast, age < 20 years, competitive sport participation, Hill-Sachs visible in external rotation, and loss of glenoid contour on AP radiographs are assigned 2 points each.
items.note: Tests exact points of the validated and widely asked ISIS scoring system.

items.q: A 64-year-old woman undergoes closed reduction of a first-time traumatic anterior glenohumeral dislocation. Post-reduction examination demonstrates persistent marked weakness of active shoulder abduction and external rotation, but sensation over the regimental badge area remains completely normal. What is the most likely diagnosis and next step in management?
o: Axillary nerve neurapraxia; conservative observation with EMG at 6 weeks
Humeral avulsion of the glenohumeral ligament (HAGL); urgent CT arthrography
Full-thickness rotator cuff tear; urgent shoulder MRI or ultrasound
items.e: In patients older than 40 (and particularly over 60, where the incidence reaches approximately 80%), persistent weakness after reduction of an anterior dislocation indicates a rotator cuff tear until proven otherwise. Immediate ultrasound or MRI is indicated to facilitate early repair.
items.note: High-yield clinical pearl matching Campbell's and exam guidelines perfectly.

items.q: A 52-year-old man presents with anterior shoulder pain and weakness after a fall onto an outstretched hand. On clinical examination, the bear-hug test is strongly positive. Based on biomechanical and clinical examination principles of the rotator cuff, the bear-hug test is most sensitive for detecting a tear of which structure?
items.e: The bear-hug test is recognized as the most sensitive clinical test for evaluating tears of the upper subscapularis tendon. In contrast, the belly-press and lift-off tests predominantly assess the mid-to-lower fibres.
items.note: Directly tested in the notes and validated by Barth et al.; accurate and high-yield.

items.q: During shoulder arthroscopy for a chronic full-thickness rotator cuff tear, a large U-shaped tear morphology is identified. According to Burkhart's biomechanical principles, which surgical step should be performed first to restore the suspension bridge load-transfer mechanism and reduce tension at the tendon-to-bone interface?
o: Medialisation of the footprint by 10 mm onto the articular cartilage
Direct transosseous-equivalent anchor fixation to the lateral footprint
Transtendon mattress suture fixation to the articular margin
items.e: For U-shaped tears, margin convergence with side-to-side suturing is performed first to convert the tear into a crescent pattern, restoring transverse force couples and dramatically decreasing strain at the lateral tendon-to-bone interface before anchor fixation.
items.note: Classic concept described by Burkhart, accurately stated in reference notes.

items.q: According to the Lafosse arthroscopic classification of subscapularis tendon tears, a complete tear involving the upper two-thirds of the subscapularis tendon with the humeral head remaining centred is classified as:
items.e: In the Lafosse classification of subscapularis tears, Type I is a partial tear of the upper third, Type II is a complete tear of the upper third, Type III is a complete tear of the upper two-thirds, Type IV is a complete tear of the entire tendon with a centred humeral head, and Type V involves an eccentric humeral head with anterior subluxation.
items.note: Standard Lafosse subscapularis classification, unambiguous single best answer.

items.q: A 42-year-old woman presents to the clinic with acute, incapacitating right shoulder pain of 48 hours' duration. Plain radiographs demonstrate an ill-defined, fluffy, cloudy translucent calcium deposit within the supraspinatus tendon. According to the Uhthoff classification, this clinical and radiographic presentation is characteristic of which phase of calcific tendinitis?
items.e: The resorptive phase of calcific tendinitis corresponds to vascular proliferation and macrophage-mediated phagocytosis; it is the most acutely painful stage and radiographically demonstrates a fluffy, ill-defined, or cloudy translucent deposit (Gärtner type III).
items.note: Accurate Uhthoff and Gärtner correlation, clear clinical vignette.

items.q: A 46-year-old manual labourer with a massive, irreparable posterosuperior rotator cuff tear, an intact subscapularis, and no glenohumeral osteoarthritis is indicated for superior capsular reconstruction (SCR). In the technique originally described by Mihata using a fascia lata autograft, what is the recommended autograft thickness to restore superior glenohumeral stability?
items.e: Mihata described superior capsular reconstruction (SCR) using a thick fascia lata autograft measuring 6 to 8 mm in thickness, which is anchored from the superior glenoid to the greater tuberosity to prevent superior humeral head migration.
items.note: High-yield factual detail from Campbell's and Mihata's seminal biomechanical papers.

items.q: A patient who underwent double-row transosseous-equivalent (suture-bridge) arthroscopic repair of a large supraspinatus tear presents at 6 months with recurrent weakness. Postoperative MRI demonstrates structural failure characterized by a tear at the musculotendinous junction medial to the medial row of anchors, with the footprint repair remaining intact. According to the Cho classification, this failure pattern is:
items.e: Cho et al. classified rotator cuff re-tears into Type 1 (failure at the footprint, most common in single-row repairs) and Type 2 (failure at the musculotendinous junction medial to the medial row of anchors, typical of overtensioned double-row/suture-bridge repairs).
items.note: Accurately represents the Cho classification of rotator cuff re-tears.

items.q: A 56-year-old patient with an irreparable posterosuperior rotator cuff tear and persistent external rotation lag is being evaluated for a latissimus dorsi tendon transfer (Gerber technique). Which of the following findings is an established contraindication to this procedure?
o: Critical shoulder angle greater than 35 degrees
items.e: Subscapularis deficiency is an established contraindication to a latissimus dorsi transfer for posterosuperior tears because an intact anterior force couple (subscapularis) is mandatory to prevent anterior or superior subluxation when the transferred latissimus fires.
items.note: Standard surgical indication/contraindication rule from Campbell's.

items.q: In the radiographic assessment of a patient with suspected rotator cuff pathology, which of the following plain radiographic findings is most strongly indicative of a massive, often irreparable rotator cuff tear?
o: Critical shoulder angle less than 30 degrees
Subchondral sclerosis of the greater tuberosity
items.e: An acromiohumeral interval (AHI) under 7 mm on an AP radiograph suggests a full-thickness rotator cuff tear, whereas an AHI under 5 mm is highly specific for a massive and often irreparable tear due to loss of the head-depressor mechanism.
items.note: Direct, unambiguous standard threshold from Campbell's and the reference text.

items.q: A 22-year-old male football player presents with insidious anterior groin pain, a positive 'C sign', and symptoms aggravated by prolonged sitting. Physical examination reveals restricted internal rotation in flexion and a positive anterior impingement (FADIR) test. Radiographs demonstrate a pistol-grip deformity and an elevated alpha angle. Which intra-articular damage pattern is characteristically produced by this condition?
o: Outside-in delamination of the anterosuperior acetabular cartilage
Isolated chondral shearing of the fovea capitis
items.e: Cam impingement is driven by an aspherical femoral head-neck junction jamming into the acetabulum during flexion and internal rotation, typically causing outside-in abrasion, chondrolabral separation, and delamination of the anterosuperior acetabular cartilage (carpet lesion/wave sign).
items.note: Accurate, exam-standard question testing cam pathology versus pincer lesion patterns.

items.q: During hip arthroscopy, establishing the anterior portal carries a significant risk of iatrogenic nerve injury. Which neural structure lies closest to this portal, located at an average distance of approximately 3 mm?
items.e: The lateral femoral cutaneous nerve is the closest structure to the anterior (and mid-anterior) portal, passing within approximately 3 mm. The superior gluteal nerve lies superior to the anterolateral portal, while the sciatic nerve is at risk near the posterolateral portal.
items.note: Direct recall of arthroscopic portal anatomy and neurovascular danger zones, fully supported.

items.q: During arthroscopic femoroplasty (osteochondroplasty) for a cam deformity, resecting bone at the posterosuperior femoral neck (12 o'clock to posterior position) should be strictly avoided to prevent osteonecrosis of the femoral head from damaging which vessels?
o: Retinacular branches of the medial femoral circumflex artery
Ascending branches of the lateral femoral circumflex artery
Deep branches of the inferior gluteal artery
items.e: The lateral epiphyseal (retinacular) vessels supplying the femoral head arise from the medial femoral circumflex artery and enter the posterosuperior head-neck junction (12 o'clock to posterior sector); over-resection here risks avascular necrosis.
items.note: Classic operative complication pearl in hip arthroscopy.

items.q: A 26-year-old female presents with groin pain and mechanical catching. Radiographic evaluation shows a lateral centre-edge angle (LCEA) of 17 degrees and a Tönnis angle of 14 degrees. Why is isolated hip arthroscopic labral debridement or capsulotomy contraindicated in this patient?
o: It causes rapid progression of heterotopic ossification
It can precipitate catastrophic iatrogenic joint instability
It inevitably results in avascular necrosis of the femoral head
It leads to severe sciatic nerve traction neurapraxia
items.e: An LCEA <20 degrees and Tönnis angle >10 degrees define acetabular dysplasia. Performing isolated arthroscopic labral debridement or unrepaired capsulotomy in dysplastic hips removes secondary stabilizers and risks catastrophic postoperative instability or dislocation; structural reorientation (PAO) is required.
items.note: Clear, clinically important management pearl emphasized in all major arthroscopy guidelines.

items.q: What is the single most common indication for revision hip arthroscopy following previous surgical management of femoroacetabular impingement?
o: Avascular necrosis of the femoral head
Residual unaddressed or under-resected bony impingement
items.e: Residual impingement due to under-resection of the cam or pincer lesion is the most frequent reason patients require revision hip arthroscopy.
items.note: Standard high-yield fact on hip arthroscopy failure modes.

items.q: In the radiographic assessment of femoroacetabular impingement, which of the following signs on a standardised AP pelvic radiograph is indicative of cranial acetabular retroversion (pincer morphology)?
o: Lateral centre-edge angle less than 20 degrees
items.e: The crossover sign (where the anterior acetabular wall projection crosses lateral to the posterior wall line superiorly) indicates cranial acetabular retroversion, a form of focal pincer impingement. An alpha angle >55 degrees indicates cam morphology, while LCEA <20 degrees and Tönnis angle >10 degrees signify dysplasia.
items.note: Well-standardized radiological sign with unambiguous answer.

items.q: A 19-year-old athlete presents with a painful, audible click in the anterior hip occurring as the hip extends and internally rotates from a flexed, abducted, and externally rotated position. Conservative care fails. If surgical release is indicated, which anatomical structure is addressed?
o: Iliotibial band over the greater trochanter
Iliopsoas tendon over the iliopectineal eminence or femoral head
Reflected head of the rectus femoris
items.e: Internal snapping hip syndrome produces an audible snap and anterior groin pain as the iliopsoas tendon translates over the femoral head or iliopectineal eminence during extension from a flexed, abducted, and externally rotated posture. When refractory, iliopsoas release is performed.
items.note: High-yield sports medicine pathology with classic dynamic description.

items.q: What was the primary conclusion of the landmark UK FASHIoN randomised controlled trial regarding the treatment of femoroacetabular impingement (FAI) syndrome?
o: Hip arthroscopy resulted in significantly greater improvement in patient-reported outcomes compared with personalised conservative care at 12 months
Personalised physiotherapy alone was superior to arthroscopic intervention at 12 months
Arthroscopic labral debridement was clinically superior to anchor-based labral refixation
Surgical hip dislocation yielded superior 12-month hip scores compared to hip arthroscopy
items.e: The UK FASHIoN trial demonstrated that hip arthroscopy led to clinically and statistically significant improvements in patient-reported hip-related quality of life compared with best conservative therapy (physiotherapy) at 12-month follow-up for FAI syndrome.
items.note: Landmark trial in sports medicine and hip preservation, frequently tested in superspeciality exams.

items.q: During elbow arthroscopy, which major nerve is situated closest (approximately 4 to 7 mm) to the anterolateral portal, requiring joint distension and elbow flexion to increase the safety margin during portal establishment?
items.e: The radial nerve (posterior interosseous nerve) is the closest major nerve to the anterolateral elbow portal, lying only 4 to 7 mm away. Fluid distension of the joint capsule along with flexing the elbow moves the nerve anteriorly away from the trocars, minimizing the risk of nerve palsy.
items.note: Factually accurate and directly supported by standard elbow arthroscopy literature and reference notes.

items.q: A 22-year-old overhead baseball pitcher undergoes MR arthrography of the elbow for medial joint pain during late cocking. The radiologist notes contrast medium tracking distally along the ulnar side beneath the insertion of the anterior bundle of the ulnar collateral ligament. This pathognomonic sign of an undersurface tear at the sublime tubercle is the:
items.e: The 'T sign' on MR arthrography represents a partial undersurface detachment of the anterior bundle of the ulnar collateral ligament (UCL) from its distal insertion at the sublime tubercle of the coronoid, allowing contrast to extend distally along the bone-ligament interface.
items.note: Factually accurate and classic entrance exam high-yield feature supported by notes.

items.q: A 24-year-old pitcher with posteromedial impingement secondary to valgus extension overload undergoes arthroscopic surgical management. What is the critical surgical guideline regarding olecranon resection to prevent iatrogenic stress on the ulnar collateral ligament?
o: Resect at least 5 mm of normal olecranon bone to prevent osteophyte recurrence
Excise only the impinged osteophyte and avoid over-resection of the normal olecranon
Perform a complete oblique olecranon osteotomy to clear the olecranon fossa
Expose and divide the transverse bundle of the ulnar collateral ligament to decompress the area
items.e: In posteromedial impingement surgery for valgus extension overload, the surgeon must excise only the osteophyte. Over-resection of normal olecranon bone significantly increases valgus strain on the already stressed ulnar collateral ligament (UCL).
items.note: Factually accurate surgical principle directly supported by notes.

items.q: A 45-year-old male athlete undergoes distal biceps tendon repair using a single-incision anterior approach with cortical button fixation. Which of the following is the most common neurological complication associated with this specific single-incision surgical approach?
items.e: Injury to the lateral antebrachial cutaneous nerve (LABCN) is the most common overall complication of distal biceps tendon repair performed through a single-incision anterior approach. In contrast, dual-incision (Boyd-Anderson) approaches carry a higher risk of heterotopic ossification and radioulnar synostosis.
items.note: Factually accurate and directly supported by Campbell's and notes.

items.q: A 15-year-old adolescent baseball pitcher presents with a symptomatic, unstable osteochondritis dissecans (OCD) lesion of the capitellum. Surgical reconstruction with an osteochondral autograft transfer (OATS) from the knee is specifically indicated over microfracture when the lesion:
o: Involves the entire ossific nucleus in a patient under 10 years of age
Involves over 50% of the capitellar width or extends to the lateral articular margin
Shows complete resolution of subchondral edema on magnetic resonance imaging
Is less than 25% of capitellar width in an asymptomatic individual
items.e: Osteochondral autograft transfer (OATS) is indicated for large capitellar OCD lesions that involve more than 50% of the capitellar width or extend to involve the lateral articular margin, where simple debridement and microfracture would result in articular collapse.
items.note: Factually accurate indication supported by notes.

items.q: A 14-year-old competitive pitcher sustains an acute valgus injury to the dominant elbow. Radiographs demonstrate an avulsion fracture of the medial epicondyle. Which of the following findings represents an absolute indication for open reduction and internal fixation?
o: Displacement of 1 mm without valgus instability
Widening of the apophyseal line by 1 mm compared to the non-dominant elbow
Incarceration of the avulsed bone fragment within the elbow joint
Associated mild strain of the flexor-pronator muscle origin
items.e: Incarceration of the medial epicondyle fragment inside the joint space is an absolute indication for operative open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF). Other strong indications, especially in throwers, include displacement over 2 mm, ulnar nerve dysfunction, and gross valgus instability.
items.note: Factually accurate standard orthopaedic indication supported by notes.

items.q: The anterior bundle of the ulnar collateral ligament (UCL) serves as the primary restraint to valgus stress at the elbow between 20 degrees and 120 degrees of flexion. Which specific band within this anterior bundle becomes tight in flexion?
items.e: The anterior bundle of the UCL consists of two distinct functional bands: the anterior band (which is tight in extension) and the posterior band (which is tight in flexion). The transverse bundle (Cooper ligament) plays no role in joint stability.
items.note: Factually accurate anatomical breakdown directly supported by notes.

items.q: During the lateral pivot-shift test of the elbow to evaluate posterolateral rotatory instability (PLRI), the examiner applies supination, valgus stress, and axial load while bringing the elbow from extension into flexion. At approximately what degree of flexion does the subluxated radial head spontaneously reduce?
items.e: In posterolateral rotatory instability (PLRI) due to LUCL deficiency, the radial head subluxates posterolaterally near full extension during the pivot-shift test. As the elbow is flexed to approximately 40 degrees, the tendon of the triceps and surrounding capsular structures pull the joint back, causing a visible/palpable reduction.
items.note: Factually accurate clinical test description supported by notes.

items.q: A professional sprinter sustains a hamstring strain. MRI demonstrates an intratendinous injury of the biceps femoris long head. According to the British Athletics Muscle Injury Classification (BAMIC), which subtype letter is assigned to intratendinous tears, and what is its clinical significance?
o: Subtype 'a'; associated with lower recurrence risk
Subtype 'c'; associated with a longer return to play and higher recurrence risk
Subtype 'c'; associated with rapid recovery within 3 to 5 days
items.e: Under the British Athletics Muscle Injury Classification (BAMIC), subtype 'c' denotes intratendinous injury, which carries a significantly longer time for return to play and a higher risk of recurrence compared to myofascial ('a') or musculotendinous ('b') injuries.
items.note: Accurate, factual question directly matching BAMIC criteria.

items.q: A 22-year-old long-distance runner presents with exercise-induced anterior leg pain that resolves with rest. Compartment pressure testing is performed. Which of the following findings satisfies the Pedowitz criteria for diagnosing chronic exertional compartment syndrome (CECS), and which nerve is at risk during surgical fasciotomy?
o: Pre-exercise pressure of 10 mmHg; Deep peroneal nerve
1-minute post-exercise pressure of 32 mmHg; Superficial peroneal nerve
5-minute post-exercise pressure of 12 mmHg; Tibial nerve
Pre-exercise pressure of 12 mmHg; Saphenous nerve
items.e: The Pedowitz criteria for CECS diagnosis require a pre-exercise pressure ≥15 mmHg, 1-minute post-exercise pressure ≥30 mmHg, or 5-minute post-exercise pressure ≥20 mmHg. During anterior and lateral compartment fasciotomy, the superficial peroneal nerve is at risk where it pierces the fascia approximately 10-12 cm proximal to the lateral malleolus.
items.note: Accurate and high-yield question covering Pedowitz diagnostic criteria and surgical anatomy.

items.q: A 19-year-old female distance runner presents with a femoral neck stress fracture. Further workup reveals features of Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (RED-S). When assessing bone mineral density (BMD) via dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) in young athletes and premenopausal females, which metric should be reported, and at what threshold is BMD considered concerning in an athlete?
items.e: Z-scores (not T-scores) must be used in premenopausal women and young athletes. A Z-score under -1.0 is concerning in athletes, while a Z-score under -2.0 indicates low BMD for age.
items.note: Factually precise regarding DXA scoring conventions in young athletes and RED-S guidelines.

items.q: Under the WADA Prohibited List, all beta-2 agonists are prohibited at all times EXCEPT specified inhaled therapeutic doses of select agents. What is the maximum permitted daily limit for inhaled salbutamol without requiring a Therapeutic Use Exemption (TUE)?
o: 1,600 µg per 24 hours (not exceeding 600 µg over any 8-hour period)
2,400 µg per 24 hours (not exceeding 800 µg over any 8-hour period)
items.e: Inhaled salbutamol is permitted up to a maximum dose of 1,600 µg per 24 hours, provided it does not exceed 600 µg over any 8-hour period. Doses exceeding this threshold require a TUE.
items.note: Factually exact according to current WADA S3 Beta-2 agonist thresholds.

items.q: A sports team physician is reviewing analgesics for athletes participating in upcoming international competitions. Which of the following narcotic analgesics was added to the WADA Prohibited List as banned IN COMPETITION starting in 2024?
items.e: Tramadol was added to the WADA Prohibited List under Category S7 (Narcotics) as prohibited in competition starting in 2024. Codeine, paracetamol, and local anaesthetics like lidocaine remain permitted.
items.note: High-yield, highly relevant recent WADA policy update question.

items.q: An 18-year-old athlete sustains a head injury during a rugby match and shows signs of a sport-related concussion. According to current consensus guidelines (SCAT6 / Amsterdam consensus), what is the mandatory immediate management regarding same-day return to play, and what is the minimum duration required per step during the graduated return-to-sport protocol?
o: Permitted same-day return if symptoms clear within 30 minutes; 12 hours per step
No return to play on the same day; at least 24 hours per step
Permitted same-day return after normal neuroimaging; 48 hours per step
No return to play on the same day; 7 days per step
items.e: The rule 'if in doubt, sit them out' dictates that an athlete with a suspected concussion must not return to play on the same day. The graduated stepwise return-to-sport protocol requires at least 24 hours for each stage.
items.note: Accurate, exam-worthy question adhering strictly to Amsterdam SCAT6 guidelines.

items.q: During a summer marathon, a runner collapses with confusion, irritability, and a measured rectal core body temperature of 40.8 °C. Which of the following is the primary immediate intervention recommended for this exertional heat stroke emergency?
o: Immediate IV administration of 50% dextrose followed by urgent transfer
On-site cold-water immersion ('cool first, transport second')
Administration of oral antipyretics and transport in an air-conditioned vehicle
Rapid transport to an emergency facility prior to initiating any cooling
items.e: Exertional heat stroke is defined by a core body temperature over 40 °C accompanied by central nervous system dysfunction. The mandatory initial treatment is immediate rapid cooling via cold-water immersion on site before transport ('cool first, transport second').
items.note: Standard sports medicine emergency question with universally accepted management protocol.

items.q: A 30-year-old water skier presents after experiencing a forced hip flexion with knee extension injury. MRI reveals a proximal hamstring avulsion. Surgical repair is indicated in active patients for which of the following injury patterns?
o: Single-tendon partial tear with 0.5 cm retraction
Complete avulsion of 3 tendons, or 2 tendons with over 2 cm retraction
Grade I myotendinous strain of the biceps femoris short head
Incomplete intramuscular fluid accumulation without retraction
items.e: Surgical repair of proximal hamstring avulsions in active patients is indicated for complete tears of all 3 tendons, or tears of 2 tendons with more than 2 cm of retraction. Early repair (within 4-6 weeks) yields superior clinical outcomes.
items.note: Standard surgical indication based on Campbell's Operative Orthopaedics and notes.

items.q: A 6-week-old female infant with a positive family history of developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH) undergoes a screening ultrasound of the left hip. Static coronal ultrasonography reveals an alpha angle of 54 degrees and a beta angle of 65 degrees. Which of the following is the correct Graf classification and recommended management?
o: Graf Type IIa; repeat ultrasound at 6 weeks to 3 months
Graf Type I; reassure parents and discharge from follow-up
Graf Type IIb; immediate application of a Pavlik harness
Graf Type III; urgent closed reduction and hip spica casting
items.e: Graf Type IIa represents physiological immaturity in infants under 3 months of age, defined by an alpha angle of 50–59 degrees and a beta angle of 55–77 degrees. Standard management is observation with a repeat ultrasound at 6 weeks to 3 months.
items.note: Accurate application of the Graf ultrasound classification and management guidelines for DDH.

items.q: A 2-month-old infant with developmental dysplasia of the hip is undergoing treatment in a Pavlik harness. At a follow-up visit, the mother reports that the child has stopped actively kicking the left leg. Examination reveals absent active knee extension and weak quadriceps contraction on the affected side. What is the most likely cause of this complication?
o: Excessive hip abduction causing avascular necrosis of the femoral head
Excessive hip flexion causing femoral nerve palsy
Insufficient hip flexion causing posterior redislocation of the hip
Overly tight shoulder straps causing brachial plexus compression
items.e: Excessive hip flexion (greater than 120 degrees) in a Pavlik harness can compress the femoral nerve, leading to femoral nerve palsy manifested by loss of active knee extension and quadriceps weakness. The harness should be adjusted or temporarily removed.
items.note: Classic exam question regarding positioning errors and nerve complications of the Pavlik harness.

items.q: In an infant older than 3 months of age evaluated for suspected developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH), which of the following physical examination findings is considered the single most reliable sign?
items.e: After about 3 months of age, soft tissues tighten and dislocated hips become fixed, causing classic dynamic provocative signs (Barlow and Ortolani) to become negative. Limited hip abduction (under 60 degrees in flexion or asymmetric abduction) becomes the most reliable clinical sign.
items.note: Standard board-level question testing physical exam changes by age in DDH.

items.q: During open reduction for a persistent developmental dislocation of the hip, several obstacles to reduction are encountered. Which extra-articular structure creates a characteristic 'hourglass' constriction of the hip capsule?
items.e: The iliopsoas tendon is an extra-articular obstacle that compresses the anterior capsule against the acetabular margin, forming the classic hourglass constriction of the joint capsule.
items.note: High-yield surgical pathoanatomy fact for pediatric orthopaedic examinations.

items.q: A 4-year-old child with cerebral palsy and posterosuperior acetabular dysplasia undergoes pelvic osteotomy. Which incomplete acetabular osteotomy hinges on the triradiate cartilage to specifically provide posterolateral coverage of the femoral head?
items.e: The Dega osteotomy is an incomplete acetabular reshaping osteotomy that hinges on the open triradiate cartilage to specifically provide posterolateral coverage, making it ideal for neuromuscular acetabular dysplasia in conditions like cerebral palsy.
items.note: Accurately differentiates pelvic osteotomies based on surgical technique and direction of coverage.

items.q: According to the Kalamchi and MacEwen classification of avascular necrosis (AVN) following treatment for developmental dysplasia of the hip, Group II changes are specifically characterized by:
o: Transient radiographic changes confined exclusively to the ossific nucleus
Lateral physeal damage resulting in a valgus tilt of the femoral head
Central physeal damage producing a short femoral neck (coxa breva)
Total head and physeal damage resulting in severe spherical distortion
items.e: In the Kalamchi and MacEwen AVN classification, Group I involves changes in the ossific nucleus only, Group II features lateral physeal damage causing a valgus tilt of the head and lateral growth arrest, Group III involves central physeal damage (coxa breva), and Group IV involves total head and physeal damage.
items.note: Standard classification question regarding post-treatment AVN in DDH.

items.q: A 10-month-old infant undergoes closed reduction under general anaesthesia for developmental dysplasia of the hip. An intraoperative arthrogram is performed to assess concentricity. What is the maximum acceptable width of the medial dye pool to confirm a concentric reduction?
items.e: On intraoperative arthrography during closed reduction for DDH, a medial dye pool width of less than 5 mm indicates an acceptable concentric reduction. A pool wider than 5 to 7 mm indicates non-concentric reduction requiring open reduction.
items.note: Exact quantitative criterion from Campbell's Operative Orthopaedics for closed reduction quality assessment.

items.q: In an adult patient undergoing total hip arthroplasty for a high developmental hip dislocation (Crowe type IV), subtrochanteric femoral shortening osteotomy is performed to prevent injury to which nerve when total limb lengthening exceeds approximately 4 cm?
items.e: When placing the acetabular component in the true acetabulum in Crowe IV high dislocations, limb lengthening exceeding about 4 cm risks traction injury to the sciatic nerve. A subtrochanteric shortening osteotomy reduces soft tissue tension and protects the sciatic nerve.
items.note: High-yield adult reconstruction/DDH sequelae question tested in SS exams.

items.q: A 6-year-old boy presents with symmetrical, simultaneous bilateral avascular necrosis of the capital femoral epiphyses on AP pelvic radiographs. Which of the following diagnoses should be most strongly suspected instead of classic Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease?
o: Unilateral Perthes disease with secondary compensation
items.e: Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease is bilateral in 10-15% of cases and typically presents asynchronously. Symmetrical, simultaneous bilateral femoral head involvement strongly suggests an alternative systemic or metabolic diagnosis such as multiple epiphyseal dysplasia (MED), hypothyroidism, Gaucher disease, or spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia.
items.note: Accurate representation of the differential for bilateral symmetrical epiphyseal involvement in children.

items.q: At what stage of Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease is the Herring lateral pillar classification evaluated, and what characterizes Group C involvement?
o: Initial stage; complete loss of medial femoral head height
Start of the fragmentation stage; less than 50% of lateral pillar height maintained
Reossification stage; lateral subluxation with Gage sign
Residual stage; flat femoral head with spherical congruency
items.e: The Herring lateral pillar classification is assessed at the start of the fragmentation stage on AP radiographs. Group C represents severe involvement where less than 50% of the lateral pillar height is maintained, carrying a poor prognosis regardless of treatment.
items.note: Standard classification question with correct timing and criteria.

items.q: An 8.5-year-old boy presents with Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease (bone age 7 years) at the fragmentation stage. Radiographs reveal a Herring Group B/C lateral pillar. Range of motion is well-maintained with abduction stretching. According to prospective trial evidence, what is the most appropriate management?
o: Petrie abduction cast immobilization for 18 months
Surgical containment via proximal femoral varus or Salter innominate osteotomy
items.e: According to the prospective study by Herring et al. (2004), children over 8 years of chronological age (and bone age over 6) with lateral pillar B or B/C hips achieve significantly better outcomes with surgical containment (proximal femoral varus osteotomy or Salter innominate osteotomy) than with non-operative management.
items.note: Evidence-based management question directly reflecting trial guidelines.

items.q: A mature patient previously treated for Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease demonstrates a flat femoral head (with over 1 cm of flat weight-bearing surface) articulating with a flat acetabulum on plain radiographs. How is this outcome classified under the Stulberg system, and what is the long-term prognosis?
o: Stulberg II; no long-term risk of osteoarthritis
Stulberg III; mild-to-moderate osteoarthritis in late adulthood
Stulberg IV; moderate osteoarthritis in middle age
items.e: Stulberg Class IV consists of a flat femoral head (over 1 cm flat weight-bearing surface) articulating with a flat acetabulum, representing aspherical congruency and leading to moderate osteoarthritis in middle age. Stulberg V features a flat head paired with a normal acetabulum (aspherical incongruency), causing severe early osteoarthritis.
items.note: Factually precise match for Stulberg Class IV radiographies and outcomes.

items.q: An 8-year-old boy presenting with short stature, body weight below the 50th percentile, and right hip pain is diagnosed with a stable slipped capital femoral epiphysis (SCFE). What is the recommended management strategy for the contralateral (left) hip?
o: Immediate prophylactic in situ single-screw fixation
Observation with serial radiographs every 6 months
Continuous abduction bracing until skeletal maturity
items.e: Atypical SCFE occurs in children under 10 years, over 16 years, or with short stature/low body weight, and strongly indicates an underlying endocrine or metabolic disorder. Because the incidence of bilateral slips is high in atypical SCFE, prophylactic in situ pinning of the unaffected contralateral hip is recommended.
items.note: Clear guidelines on prophylactic pinning indications in atypical SCFE.

items.q: During in situ single cannulated screw fixation for a stable slipped capital femoral epiphysis (SCFE), which technical measure is vital to avoid joint penetration and subsequent chondrolysis?
o: Placing the entry point inferior to the lesser trochanter
Engaging at least 8 to 10 threads across the physis
Maintaining the screw tip at least 5 mm from subchondral bone using the approach-withdraw technique under multiple fluoroscopic views
Positioning the screw in the posterosuperior aspect of the femoral neck
items.e: Unrecognised screw penetration is the commonest cause of chondrolysis. To prevent joint penetration, the screw tip must remain at least 5 mm from subchondral bone, confirmed in multiple fluoroscopic views using the 'approach-withdraw' technique.
items.note: Surgical technique pearl accurately described.

items.q: Which radiographic sign of slipped capital femoral epiphysis (SCFE) describes the loss of the normal triangular overlap between the medial femoral metaphysis and the posterior acetabular wall on an AP pelvis view?
items.e: Capener sign is defined as the loss of the normal triangular overlap between the medial femoral metaphysis and the posterior acetabular wall on an AP radiograph. Metaphyseal blanch sign of Steel represents double density from epiphyseal-metaphyseal overlap, and failure of Klein line to intersect the epiphysis is Trethowan sign.
items.note: Standard radiographic eponym/sign matching question.

items.q: A 14-year-old boy with severe chronic stable SCFE has residual symptomatic structural deformity. Which osteotomy level provides compensatory deformity correction while carrying the lowest risk of avascular necrosis (AVN) of the femoral head?
o: Subcapital realignment via modified Dunn procedure
items.e: Intertrochanteric osteotomy (such as the Imhäuser flexion-valgus-internal rotation osteotomy) is performed well away from the retinacular vessels, making it the safest osteotomy for preserving femoral head blood supply and avoiding AVN, though it provides compensatory rather than anatomic correction.
items.note: Accurate comparison of osteotomy levels and AVN risks in SCFE.

items.q: A 4-year-old child with neglected idiopathic clubfoot undergoes surgical posteromedial soft-tissue release. The operating surgeon takes extra care to protect the posterior tibial artery because which of the following vessels is hypoplastic or absent in approximately 85% of CTEV feet?
items.e: In congenital talipes equinovarus (CTEV), hypoplasia or absence of the anterior tibial artery occurs in approximately 85% of cases. Thus, intraoperative preservation of the posterior tibial artery is vital during soft-tissue surgical procedures.
items.note: Accurate, factual high-yield clinical question fully aligned with standard orthopaedic texts.

items.q: A newborn with bilateral clubfoot is evaluated prior to Ponseti casting using the Pirani scoring system. Which of the following signs is evaluated as part of the Midfoot Contracture Score (MFCS)?
o: Lateral head of the talus coverage
items.e: The Pirani score has a maximum of 6 points split into two 3-point subscales: Midfoot Contracture Score (MFCS) and Hindfoot Contracture Score (HFCS). MFCS includes curved lateral border, medial crease, and lateral head of the talus coverage, whereas HFCS includes posterior crease, empty heel, and rigid equinus.
items.note: Factually accurate classification detail commonly asked in SS entrance exams.

items.q: A 3.5-year-old child previously treated for clubfoot with Ponseti serial casting presents with dynamic supination during gait due to an overactive tibialis anterior muscle. Clinical examination shows a flexible foot deformity, and radiographs demonstrate an ossified lateral cuneiform. What is the surgical procedure of choice?
o: Tibialis anterior tendon transfer to the lateral cuneiform
Tibialis posterior tendon transfer to the navicular
Evans calcaneocuboid fusion and lateral column shortening
items.e: Dynamic supination in a relapsed clubfoot is driven by an overactive tibialis anterior muscle. In a child over 2.5–3 years of age with a flexible foot and an ossified lateral (third) cuneiform, tibialis anterior tendon transfer (TATT) to the lateral cuneiform is the definitive treatment.
items.note: Standard board-style vignette with unambiguous management indication.

items.q: Which radiographic stress view reliably differentiates congenital vertical talus (CVT) from congenital oblique talus?
o: Standing AP radiograph showing talocalcaneal parallelism
Forced dorsiflexion lateral view showing persistent equinus
Forced maximal plantarflexion lateral view showing non-reduction of the talonavicular joint
45-degree internal oblique view showing an elongated anterior calcaneal process
items.e: The diagnostic radiograph for congenital vertical talus (CVT) is the forced maximal plantarflexion lateral view, where the talar axis line remains plantar to the first metatarsal axis because the talonavicular dislocation is irreducible. In congenital oblique talus, the talonavicular dislocation reduces on maximal plantarflexion.
items.note: High-yield diagnostic concept correctly framed and options are clear.

items.q: In the Dobbs method ('reverse Ponseti') for non-operative management of congenital vertical talus (CVT), serial manipulation and casting of the forefoot are performed in which direction before percutaneous pinning and Achilles tenotomy?
items.e: The Dobbs technique ('reverse Ponseti') for congenital vertical talus corrects the deformity by serial manipulation and casting with the forefoot placed in plantarflexion and inversion while applying counter-pressure on the talar head, followed by percutaneous talonavicular pinning and Achilles tenotomy.
items.note: Factually precise description of the Dobbs method.

items.q: An 11-year-old child presents with a painful rigid flatfoot and recurrent ankle sprains. A 45-degree internal oblique radiograph demonstrates an 'anteater nose sign' representing an elongated anterior process of the calcaneus. What is the diagnosis?
items.e: Calcaneonavicular (CN) coalition is the most common tarsal coalition (~53%), presenting typically between 8 and 12 years of age with a rigid painful flatfoot or sprains. The classic radiographic feature on a 45-degree internal oblique view is the 'anteater nose sign', caused by elongation of the anterior process of the calcaneus towards the navicular.
items.note: Classic radiological sign question, completely factual and accurate.

items.q: In an 11-year-old child with Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease presenting with a bilateral cavovarus foot deformity, a Coleman block test demonstrates complete correction of the hindfoot varus to neutral when standing with a block under the lateral heel and foot. What does this finding indicate?
o: Fixed hindfoot varus requiring calcaneal osteotomy
Rigid midfoot cavus requiring triple arthrodesis
items.e: The Coleman block test assesses hindfoot flexibility in a cavovarus foot. Correction of hindfoot varus when the lateral foot is supported (allowing the plantarflexed first ray to drop) indicates that the hindfoot varus is flexible and forefoot-driven, meaning management can focus on forefoot procedures without needing calcaneal osteotomy.
items.note: High-yield clinical interpretation of Coleman block test.

items.q: A newborn infant presenting with severe non-idiopathic bilateral clubfoot is noted to have characteristic 'hitchhiker's thumbs' and 'cauliflower ears'. Which underlying syndromic condition is responsible for this presentation?
items.e: Diastrophic dysplasia is a cause of syndromic/non-idiopathic clubfoot characteristically associated with 'hitchhiker's thumbs' (abducted thumbs) and 'cauliflower ears' (due to cystic swelling of the pinna).
items.note: Classic syndrome association question in paediatric orthopaedics.

items.q: A 6-year-old child presents with a completely displaced extension-type supracondylar fracture of the humerus. Radiographs show posterolateral displacement of the distal fragment (proximal spike directed anteromedially). Which neurovascular structures are at highest risk of injury in this displacement pattern?
o: Ulnar nerve and anterior interosseous artery
Radial nerve and profundus brachii artery
items.e: In extension-type supracondylar fractures with posterolateral displacement of the distal fragment, the proximal fragment spike projects anteromedially, placing the median nerve and brachial artery at highest risk. Posteromedial displacement risks the radial nerve.
items.note: Accurate anatomical correlation for extension-type supracondylar fracture displacement patterns.

items.q: A 12-year-old child weighing 52 kg sustains a closed length-stable femoral shaft fracture. When performing rigid intramedullary nailing, which entry site must be avoided to prevent osteonecrosis of the femoral head?
items.e: Piriformis entry is strictly avoided in paediatric femoral nailing because the lateral ascending cervical branches of the medial femoral circumflex artery pass near the piriformis fossa; injury to these vessels risks avascular necrosis of the femoral head. A lateral trochanteric entry is preferred.
items.note: Standard surgical guideline regarding intramedullary nail entry sites in older children/adolescents.

items.q: A 9-year-old child presents with a partial distal femoral physeal arrest (physeal bar) following trauma. Surgical resection of the physeal bar with interposition is indicated if the bar involves less than what percentage of the physis and the child has at least how much growth remaining?
o: Under 25% of the physis and at least 1 year (~1 cm) of growth left
Under 50% of the physis and at least 2 years (~2 cm) of growth left
Under 50% of the physis and at least 4 years (~4 cm) of growth left
Under 75% of the physis and at least 3 years (~3 cm) of growth left
items.e: Surgical resection of a physeal bar with interposition (fat or cement) is indicated if the bar involves under 50% of the physis and the child has at least 2 years (approximately 2 cm) of growth left. If >50% is involved or <2 years remain, complete epiphysiodesis is indicated.
items.note: Standard management criteria for physeal bar resection versus epiphysiodesis.

items.q: A 7-year-old boy presents with an elbow injury. Radiographs reveal a lateral condyle fracture of the distal humerus displaced by 3.5 mm. Which treatment approach is indicated, and which anatomical surgical precaution must be observed to prevent avascular necrosis?
o: Above-elbow cast immobilization; avoid hyperflexing the elbow in cast
Open reduction and internal fixation; avoid posterior soft-tissue dissection
Closed percutaneous pinning; avoid placing pins through the lateral epicondyle
Fragment excision; avoid division of the anterior capsule
items.e: Lateral condyle fractures displaced over 2 mm require open reduction and internal fixation. Posterior dissection must be strictly avoided during ORIF because the blood supply to the condyle enters posteriorly, and stripping it risks avascular necrosis.
items.note: Correct treatment indication and classic surgical pitfall for paediatric lateral condyle fractures.

items.q: During a Salter-Harris physeal fracture, the fracture line typically propagates through which zone of the growth plate, allowing germinal cells to remain attached to the epiphysis?
items.e: Physeal fractures typically propagate through the hypertrophic zone (the weakest region of the growth plate). The germinal cells (reserve and proliferative zones) remain with the epiphyseal fragment, which is why most physeal fractures grow normally.
items.note: High-yield basic science knowledge on growth plate anatomy and Salter-Harris fractures.

items.q: A 4-year-old child sustains an undisplaced proximal tibial metaphyseal fracture that is treated in a long-leg cast. One year later, the parents return concerned about a progressive cosmetic deformity at the knee. Which classic deformity occurs following this injury (Cozen fracture)?
items.e: Proximal tibial metaphyseal fractures in young children (Cozen fracture) frequently develop progressive genu valgum over the subsequent year due to asymmetric medial overgrowth. Parents should be warned beforehand, and early osteotomy should be avoided as most cases remodel.
items.note: Classic presentation and natural history of Cozen fracture of the proximal tibia.

items.q: A 6-year-old child undergoes closed reduction and percutaneous pinning for a completely displaced supracondylar fracture of the humerus. Post-reduction examination reveals a pink, warm hand with capillary refill under 2 seconds, but the radial pulse is absent. There are no motor or sensory neurological deficits. What is the most appropriate initial management?
o: Urgent open exploration of the brachial artery via an anterior approach
Immediate removal of lateral pins and re-manipulation in hyperflexion
Admission, limb elevation, and close clinical observation
items.e: A 'pink pulseless hand' (perfused hand without palpable pulse) after closed reduction should be managed with admission, limb elevation, and close observation. Urgent open arterial exploration is indicated only if perfusion deteriorates (white pulseless hand) or if there is an associated median nerve palsy.
items.note: Core management protocol for vascular status following supracondylar fracture reduction.

items.q: In an ambulatory child with spastic diplegic cerebral palsy presenting with a stiff-knee gait during the swing phase, rectus femoris transfer is performed to eliminate its inappropriate swing-phase extension moment. To which of the following tendons is the rectus femoris tendon most commonly transferred posterolaterally?
o: Patellar tendon proximal to its insertion
items.e: In stiff-knee gait caused by rectus femoris spasticity during swing, the distal rectus femoris tendon is freed from the patella and transferred posterolaterally to the semitendinosus, gracilis, or sartorius tendon. This converts its vector to prevent stance phase stiffness while eliminating swing phase extension.
items.note: Accurate standard technique described in Campbell's and Tachdjian's for stiff-knee gait in CP.

items.q: A 6-year-old child with spastic quadriplegic cerebral palsy is found to have a Reimers migration index of 45% on a routine hip surveillance radiograph, accompanied by moderate acetabular dysplasia. What is the most appropriate surgical reconstruction to restore hip containment and prevent dislocation?
o: Isolation and neurectomy of the obturator nerve alone
Varus derotation osteotomy (VDRO) of the proximal femur combined with pelvic osteotomy
items.e: A Reimers migration index greater than 30% indicates hip subluxation, and values exceeding 40% with acetabular dysplasia in a young child mandate reconstructive bony surgery (proximal femoral varus derotation osteotomy combined with a pelvic osteotomy such as a Dega or San Diego procedure) to maintain joint congruity.
items.note: Standard hip surveillance and surgical management protocol for hip subluxation in cerebral palsy.

items.q: A 4-year-old child with myelomeningocele is able to walk community distances using ankle-foot orthoses (AFOs). Physical examination shows active hip flexion, hip adduction, knee extension, and ankle dorsiflexion (active tibialis anterior), but absent ankle plantarflexion and weak hip abduction. What is the functional motor level of this patient's spinal lesion?
items.e: The L4 motor level in myelomeningocele is characterized by functional knee extension (quadriceps) and active ankle dorsiflexion (tibialis anterior present), but absent ankle plantarflexors (gastrocnemius-soleus complex, which corresponds to S1) and weak gluteus medius.
items.note: Standard Hoffer / standard pediatric orthopaedic functional motor level classification for myelomeningocele.

items.q: A 9-year-old child with spastic hemiplegic cerebral palsy demonstrates a dynamic equinovarus foot deformity exclusively during the swing phase of gait due to overactivity of the tibialis anterior muscle. Which surgical procedure is specifically indicated?
o: Split anterior tibialis tendon transfer (SPLATT) to the lateral cuneiform or cuboid
Split posterior tibialis tendon transfer (SPOTT) to the Achilles tendon
Plantar fascia release with calcaneal lengthening osteotomy
items.e: Split anterior tibialis tendon transfer (SPLATT) is indicated for dynamic swing-phase varus in cerebral palsy driven by an overactive tibialis anterior. Splitting the tendon and moving the lateral half to the cuboid or lateral cuneiform balances the dorsiflexion moment across the ankle.
items.note: Classic indication and procedure for dynamic swing-phase varus in cerebral palsy.

items.q: Regarding the natural history and orthopaedic management of spinal deformity in boys with Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD), which of the following statements is CORRECT?
o: Thoracolumbosacral orthoses (TLSO) effectively prevent curve progression long-term
Spinal fusion should be delayed until the Cobb angle exceeds 70 degrees
Loss of independent ambulation is strongly associated with rapid acceleration of scoliosis curve progression
Corticosteroid therapy increases the overall incidence of scoliosis requiring surgery
items.e: Scoliosis in DMD progresses rapidly once boys lose independent ambulation and become wheelchair-bound. Bracing does not prevent curve progression in DMD, and posterior spinal fusion is indicated early (often around 20-30 degrees Cobb angle) before forced vital capacity markedly declines.
items.note: Accurate natural history and treatment principles for DMD spinal deformity in standard textbooks.

items.q: Crouch gait in cerebral palsy is characterized by excessive knee flexion, hip flexion, and ankle dorsiflexion during the stance phase of gait. Which surgical complication is a well-known iatrogenic cause of crouch gait?
o: Over-lengthening of the Achilles tendon (heel cord)
Posterolateral transfer of the rectus femoris
Iliopsoas recession at the pelvic brim
items.e: Isolated or excessive lengthening of the Achilles tendon destroys the plantarflexion-knee extension couple. This leads to calcaneus ankle deformity, loss of push-off, and secondary excessive knee and hip flexion (iatrogenic crouch gait).
items.note: Classic iatrogenic complication well-documented in cerebral palsy gait literature and textbooks.

items.q: In an adolescent patient with Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease and a cavovarus foot deformity, the Coleman block test shows complete correction of the hindfoot varus to neutral when the first metatarsal head is allowed to drop off the lateral side of the block. What does this result indicate?
o: Rigid hindfoot varus deformity requiring triple arthrodesis
Flexible hindfoot varus driven primarily by a plantarflexed first metatarsal
Isolated spasticity of the gastrocnemius muscle
items.e: The Coleman block test evaluates the flexibility of hindfoot varus. Correction of hindfoot varus when the first ray drops off the block confirms that the heel varus is flexible and forefoot-driven (caused by a plantarflexed first ray from peroneus longus overactivity).
items.note: Standard interpretation of the Coleman block test in neuromuscular cavovarus foot evaluation.

items.q: A neonate with Arthrogryposis Multiplex Congenita presents with bilateral rigid clubfeet (talipes equinovarus). Which feature distinguishes arthrogrypotic clubfoot from idiopathic clubfoot?
o: Excellent response to standard Ponseti manipulation alone with zero relapse risk
Normal histological structure of surrounding periarticular soft tissue structures
Low rate of recurrence after posteromedial soft tissue release
