High rigidity and resistance to correction, with frequent relapse requiring extensive soft tissue releases or talectomy
items.e: Arthrogrypotic clubfeet are severely rigid due to periarticular fibrosis and myodysplasia. They are resistant to non-operative measures alone, have very high recurrence rates after initial correction, and frequently require extensive soft-tissue releases, talectomy, or Ilizarov correction.
items.note: Standard textbook pathognomonic feature distinguishing non-idiopathic arthrogrypotic clubfoot.

items.q: A 2-year-old child presents with disproportionate short stature, rhizomelic limb shortening, frontal bossing, midface hypoplasia, and a trident hand appearance. Radiographic evaluation of the spine and pelvis is performed. Which of the following radiographic findings is characteristic of this condition?
o: Interpedicular distance that widens progressively from L1 to L5
Interpedicular distance that narrows progressively from L1 to L5
Platyspondyly with a heaped-up posterior vertebral body
Symmetric diaphyseal cortical hyperostosis and sclerosis
items.e: In achondroplasia, a characteristic radiographic feature of the lumbar spine is progressive narrowing of the interpedicular distance from L1 down to L5, unlike normal spines where the interpedicular distance widens. Other classic pelvic and spinal features include squared iliac wings, a champagne-glass pelvic inlet, and posterior vertebral scalloping.
items.note: The question accurately tests a pathognomonic radiographic sign of achondroplasia as described in the reference notes.

items.q: A 6-year-old child diagnosed with Morquio syndrome (Mucopolysaccharidoses type IV) is scheduled for elective reconstructive foot surgery under general anesthesia. Which of the following preoperative screening evaluations is essential prior to induction of anesthesia?
o: Flexion-extension cervical spine radiographs to evaluate for upper cervical instability
Dynamic stress radiographs of both hips to rule out coxa vara
Technetium-99m bone scan to detect skeletal exostoses
items.e: Preoperative upper cervical instability screening (flexion-extension radiographs with or without MRI) is mandatory prior to anesthesia in Morquio syndrome, SED congenita, pseudoachondroplasia, Down syndrome, Larsen syndrome, and metatropic dysplasia due to high risk of odontoid hypoplasia and atlantoaxial subluxation.
items.note: This is a critical safety fact emphasized in the reference notes for several dysplasias including Morquio and SED.

items.q: A 7-year-old child presents with mild short stature, joint stiffness, and bilateral hip pain. Radiographs demonstrate small, irregular, flattened femoral epiphyses affecting both hips symmetrically at the exact same radiographical stage. The spine appears radiographically normal. Which feature most reliably differentiates Multiple Epiphyseal Dysplasia (MED) from bilateral Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease?
o: Asynchronous progression of femoral head osteonecrosis at different stages
Bilateral, symmetrical femoral head involvement at the same radiographic stage with normal spine radiograph
Anterior inferior beaking of the lumbar vertebral bodies
A champagne-glass appearance of the pelvic inlet
items.e: Multiple Epiphyseal Dysplasia (MED) characteristically presents with bilateral, symmetrical femoral head involvement at the exact same stage of epiphyseal change and a normal spine. In contrast, bilateral Perthes disease is typically asynchronous, presenting at different radiographic stages of disease between the two hips.
items.note: The question correctly identifies the key clinical differentiator between these two common pediatric hip conditions.

items.q: A 5-year-old child presents with the ability to bring both shoulders together anteriorly in the midline of the chest. Clinical examination reveals supernumerary teeth and delayed tooth eruption. Radiographs demonstrate persistent open cranial sutures with wormian bones and a widened symphysis pubis. Which gene mutation is responsible for this skeletal dysplasia?
items.e: Cleidocranial dysplasia is an autosomal dominant condition caused by mutations in the RUNX2 (CBFA1) gene, which is the master gene for osteoblast differentiation. Characteristic features include absent or hypoplastic clavicles (allowing shoulder hypermobility), open fontanelles with wormian bones, supernumerary teeth, coxa vara, and a wide symphysis pubis.
items.note: The clinical triad of clavicular hypoplasia, dental anomalies, and wormian bones is classic for cleidocranial dysplasia and its association with RUNX2.

items.q: A 4-year-old boy presents with mild short stature, a waddling gait, genu varum, and bilateral coxa vara. Radiographs show metaphyseal flaring and irregularity of the proximal femora and distal knees with normal spinal alignment. Laboratory evaluation reveals normal serum levels of calcium, phosphate, alkaline phosphatase, and 25-hydroxyvitamin D. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.e: Schmid type metaphyseal chondrodysplasia (COL10A1 mutation, AD) presents clinically and radiographically similar to rickets (short stature, genu varum, coxa vara, metaphyseal flaring). However, it is distinguished from rickets by completely normal serum levels of calcium, phosphate, alkaline phosphatase, and vitamin D.
items.note: The question tests the essential differential diagnosis of rickets-like metaphyseal changes with normal biochemistry.

items.q: A 9-month-old infant with multiple café-au-lait spots is evaluated for anterolateral bowing of the left tibia. Radiographs reveal cortical thinning of the diaphysis without an overt fracture line or pseudarthrosis. What is the most appropriate initial orthopaedic management strategy?
o: Immediate corrective osteotomy and intramedullary rodding
Excision of the bowed segment and Ilizarov bone transport
Vascularised fibular grafting of the affected diaphysis
Protection in a total contact orthosis to prevent fracture
items.e: Anterolateral bowing of the tibia in infants (frequently associated with NF1) indicates impending pseudarthrosis. The affected tibia must be protected with a custom total contact orthosis to prevent fracture; prophylactic osteotomy of the bowed tibia is contraindicated as it inevitably leads to nonunion.
items.note: The question correctly identifies the conservative management of pre-fracture tibial bowing in NF1, avoiding contraindicated osteotomies.

items.q: An 18-year-old male with a known diagnosis of Hereditary Multiple Exostoses (HME) presents with new-onset pain and enlargement of a long-standing lesion in his proximal femur. MRI demonstrates a cartilage cap thickness of 2.5 cm. What is the primary concern indicated by these clinical and imaging features?
o: Acute pathological fracture through an osteolytic lesion
Infection with secondary osteomyelitis of the lesion
items.e: In patients with Hereditary Multiple Exostoses, warning signs of malignant transformation to secondary chondrosarcoma include new onset of pain, lesion enlargement after skeletal maturity, and a cartilage cap thickness greater than 2 cm on MRI in adults.
items.note: The question uses standard criteria (age, pain, cap thickness) for identifying malignant change in HME.

items.q: A newborn child is evaluated for short-limbed dwarfism, bilateral rigid clubfeet, cystic ear swellings ("cauliflower ears"), a cleft palate, and short, proximally placed, abducted thumbs ("hitchhiker thumbs"). Which gene defect is associated with this autosomal recessive disorder?
items.e: Diastrophic dysplasia is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in the SLC26A2 sulfate transporter gene. Key clinical features include short stature, hitchhiker thumbs (short, abducted 1st metacarpals), cauliflower ears (cystic swellings in infancy), rigid clubfeet, cleft palate, and progressive spine deformities.
items.note: The question correctly links the classic clinical features of diastrophic dysplasia to its specific genetic mutation.

items.q: A 3-year-old child presents with a limp and low-grade fever. C-reactive protein (CRP) and White Blood Cell (WBC) count are only mildly elevated. Joint fluid aspiration shows 40,000 WBC/mm3, but the Gram stain is negative. Which organism, often requiring PCR or inoculation into blood-culture bottles for detection, is the most likely cause in this age group?
items.e: Kingella kingae is the most common cause of osteoarticular infection in children aged 6 months to 4 years when PCR is used. It typically presents with mild illness and low-grade markers, and it grows poorly on standard media.
items.note: The clinical presentation (mild markers, negative Gram stain, age group) is classic for Kingella kingae as described in the reference notes.

items.q: A 10-year-old with sickle cell disease presents with persistent fever and localized tenderness over the femoral diaphysis. Blood cultures grow Salmonella. What is the characteristic mechanism described for this organism seeding the bone in sickle cell patients?
o: Direct inoculation from a puncture wound through a sneaker
Contiguous spread from a psoas abscess
Bowel infarcts allowing translocation and bacteraemia
Defective phagocytosis in the metaphyseal sinusoids
items.e: In sickle cell disease, Salmonella is a characteristic pathogen because bowel infarcts allow the bacteria to translocate into the bloodstream, leading to haematogenous seeding of the bone.
items.note: The mechanism of Salmonella translocation in sickle cell patients is a standard orthopaedic fact supported by the notes.

items.q: In the surgical management of chronic osteomyelitis in a child, a sequestrectomy is planned. Which of the following is the most critical prerequisite to prevent a pathological fracture or segmental bone loss during this procedure?
o: Normalization of the ESR and CRP
Identification of the 'paprika sign' during debridement
Presence of a sufficiently strong and mature involucrum
Wait until all cloacae have spontaneously closed
items.e: Sequestrectomy should be delayed until the involucrum (the new bone laid down by the periosteum) is strong enough to support the limb to prevent segmental loss or fracture.
items.note: The timing of sequestrectomy relative to involucrum formation is a critical surgical principle in paediatric chronic osteomyelitis.

items.q: A 1-month-old neonate in the NICU is found to have pseudoparalysis of the left hip. Radiographs suggest a combined osteomyelitis of the proximal femoral metaphysis and septic arthritis. Which anatomical feature explains this combined involvement in this age group?
o: Absence of a subperiosteal space in neonates
Firm attachment of the paediatric periosteum
items.e: In children under approximately 18 months of age, transphyseal vessels cross the physis, allowing metaphyseal infection to spread directly to the epiphysis and the joint.
items.note: The role of transphyseal vessels in neonatal bone infection is a fundamental pathophysiology concept.

items.q: A 6-year-old boy is evaluated for hip pain. He is non-weight-bearing, has a temperature of 39°C, and an ESR of 55 mm/h. His WBC count is 11,000/mm3. According to the Kocher criteria, what is the predicted probability that this child has septic arthritis of the hip?
items.e: The child meets 3 of the 4 Kocher criteria: non-weight-bearing, temperature >38.5°C, and ESR >40 mm/h. The WBC count (11,000) is below the 12,000 threshold. The probability for 3 criteria is approximately 93%.
items.note: The question tests the application of the Kocher criteria, a high-yield exam topic, using the specific thresholds and probabilities provided in the notes.

items.q: A child with acute haematogenous osteomyelitis is being treated with IV antibiotics. Which of the following laboratory parameters is the best marker of response to monitor and guide the switch to oral therapy?
items.e: CRP rises and falls rapidly, usually normalizing within a week of effective treatment. It is the best marker to monitor response; a 50% reduction is often used to guide the switch to oral antibiotics.
items.note: CRP's role as the primary monitoring tool for osteomyelitis treatment response is well-established in the Peltola trials and standard texts.

items.q: An 11-year-old girl presents with recurrent episodes of bone pain involving the medial clavicle and distal tibia. Biopsy shows chronic inflammation but cultures are sterile. She also has palmoplantar pustulosis. What is the first-line medical treatment for this condition?
o: Surgical debridement of all involved sites
items.e: This is a classic presentation of Chronic Recurrent Multifocal Osteomyelitis (CRMO). It is an autoinflammatory condition with sterile cultures, often involving the medial clavicle. NSAIDs are the first-line treatment.
items.note: The question correctly identifies the clinical features and first-line management of CRMO as per the reference notes.

items.q: During the repair of flexor tendons in 'No Man's Land' (Zone II), which pulleys are considered the most critical to preserve to prevent bowstringing and ensure efficient mechanical advantage?
items.e: The A2 (proximal phalanx) and A4 (middle phalanx) pulleys are the most biomechanically important annular pulleys. They prevent bowstringing of the flexor tendons; preserving or reconstructing them is essential for digit function.
items.note: The question is factually correct and tests a fundamental principle of hand surgery mentioned in the reference notes.

items.q: A patient presents with paradoxical extension of the PIP joint while attempting to flex the finger following a distal FDP laceration. This clinical phenomenon is caused by:
o: Over-advancement of the FDP tendon (Quadriga effect)
Tethering of the lumbrical muscle pulling the extensor apparatus
items.e: The Lumbrical-plus finger occurs when the FDP is cut distal to the lumbrical origin. When the patient attempts to flex, the FDP pulls the lumbrical proximally, which in turn pulls the extensor apparatus, causing paradoxical IP extension.
items.note: Correctly identifies the mechanism of the lumbrical-plus phenomenon as described in the notes.

items.q: A 22-year-old sustains a human bite over the third MCP joint during a fight. Which of the following is the most appropriate antibiotic choice to cover the characteristic organism associated with this injury?
items.e: Fight bites are associated with Eikenella corrodens, which is typically resistant to first-generation cephalosporins, clindamycin, and penicillinase-resistant penicillins. Co-amoxiclav is the treatment of choice.
items.note: Accurately reflects the microbiology and pharmacological management of fight bites.

items.q: A patient with suspected acute central slip rupture of the PIP joint is evaluated using the Elson test. Which finding is diagnostic of a complete central slip disruption?
o: The DIP joint remains floppy during resisted PIP extension
The DIP joint becomes rigid and extends during resisted PIP extension
Inability to extend the MCP joint
Ulnar deviation of the finger during flexion
items.e: In a positive Elson test (central slip rupture), the lateral bands compensate for the lack of PIP extension. When the PIP is flexed 90 degrees and extension is resisted, the lateral bands act on the DIP joint, making it rigid and extended.
items.note: Correctly describes the positive finding of the Elson test for central slip injury.

items.q: A 10-year-old child presents with an open mallet injury and an associated transverse fracture through the physis of the distal phalanx. What is this injury called and what is the priority in management?
o: Seymour fracture; Irrigation, debridement, and nail-bed repair
items.e: A Seymour fracture is a juxta-epiphyseal fracture of the distal phalanx (often open with nail-bed injury). It is considered an open fracture and requires formal irrigation, debridement, and nail-bed repair to prevent osteomyelitis.
items.note: Correctly identifies the eponym and the critical management steps for this pediatric hand injury.

items.q: Which of the following statements regarding flexor tendon repair strength and rehabilitation is correct?
o: The strength of the repair is primarily determined by the epitendinous suture
A 2-strand core suture is sufficient for early active motion protocols
The repair is at its weakest between 7 to 14 days post-operatively
Dorsally placed core sutures are weaker than volar sutures
items.e: Tendon repair strength falls considerably in the first 10-21 days due to softening; ruptures most commonly occur between days 7 and 14. Multi-strand (4-6 strand) core sutures are required for early active motion.
items.note: Tests the critical timeline of tendon healing and repair strength mentioned in Campbell's and the notes.

items.q: Intersection syndrome, a condition causing pain and swelling in the distal forearm, occurs where the muscles of the first dorsal compartment (APL and EPB) cross over which tendons?
items.e: Intersection syndrome occurs about 4-8 cm proximal to Lister's tubercle, where the APL and EPB (1st compartment) cross over the ECRL and ECRB (2nd compartment) tendons.
items.note: Correctly identifies the anatomical basis of intersection syndrome.

items.q: A 28-year-old male sustained a high-energy crush injury to his forearm. Intra-operative exploration reveals a nerve that appears to be in continuity with a bulky neuroma, but the epineurium is intact. Histology of such a lesion (Sunderland Grade IV) would show disruption of which of the following structures?
items.e: In a Sunderland Grade IV injury (neuroma-in-continuity), the axon, endoneurium, and perineurium are all disrupted, but the epineurium remains intact. This injury requires excision and repair/grafting as spontaneous recovery does not occur.
items.note: The question accurately tests the Sunderland classification based on the provided notes and standard orthopaedic literature.

items.q: During a carpal tunnel release, a surgeon must be particularly cautious of the recurrent motor branch of the median nerve. Which anatomical variant of this branch is most at risk because it passes directly through the transverse carpal ligament?
items.e: The transligamentous variant occurs in approximately 25% of individuals and is particularly at risk during surgical release of the flexor retinaculum. The extraligamentous variant is the most common (50%).
items.note: The question correctly identifies the anatomical variant at highest risk during surgery as per the reference notes.

items.q: A 45-year-old patient presents with numbness in the little finger and the ulnar side of the ring finger. Physical examination reveals sensory loss over the dorsoulnar aspect of the hand. Which of the following is the most likely site of ulnar nerve compression?
items.e: In cubital tunnel syndrome, sensation over the dorsoulnar hand is lost because the dorsal cutaneous branch of the ulnar nerve arises 5-8 cm proximal to the wrist. In Guyon's canal compression, this branch is spared, and dorsal sensation remains normal.
items.note: The question tests the clinical differentiation between proximal (elbow) and distal (wrist) ulnar nerve compression using the dorsal cutaneous branch.

items.q: A patient with suspected pronator syndrome reports symptoms are specifically exacerbated by resisted flexion of the proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joint of the middle finger. This suggests the site of median nerve compression is at the:
o: Two heads of the pronator teres
items.e: Resisted middle finger PIP joint flexion specifically tests the FDS arch (sublimis bridge) as a compression site. Resisted pronation with elbow extension tests the pronator teres heads, while resisted elbow flexion with supination tests the lacertus fibrosus.
items.note: The provocative tests for pronator syndrome sites are correctly matched to the FDS arch as per the reference notes.

items.q: A patient with rheumatoid arthritis is unable to actively extend the fingers at the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joints. The surgeon performs a tenodesis test: passive flexion of the wrist results in passive extension of the MCP joints. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.e: A positive tenodesis test (passive MCP extension upon wrist flexion) indicates that the extensor tendons are intact, pointing toward PIN palsy. If the tendons were ruptured (common in RA), the fingers would remain flexed regardless of wrist position.
items.note: The question correctly uses the tenodesis test to differentiate between neurological palsy and mechanical tendon rupture in a clinical scenario.

items.q: What is the most appropriate management for a 2 cm nerve gap in a small-calibre sensory nerve of the hand when a primary tension-free repair cannot be achieved?
items.e: Nerve conduits (hollow tubes) are indicated for small-calibre sensory nerve gaps of less than about 3 cm. For larger gaps (up to 5-7 cm) or larger nerves, processed allografts or autografts (sural nerve) are preferred.
items.note: The management of nerve gaps based on size and nerve type is accurately reflected from the reference notes.

items.q: In the surgical management of a high radial nerve palsy, which of the following represents a synergistic tendon transfer to restore finger extension?
items.e: Synergistic transfers utilize muscles that naturally contract together; wrist flexion is synergistic with finger extension. Therefore, transferring a wrist flexor (FCU or FCR) to the finger extensors (EDC) is easier for the patient to retrain.
items.note: The question correctly identifies the synergistic relationship between wrist flexors and finger extensors in tendon transfer principles.

items.q: A patient with a traumatic brachial plexus injury presents with complete sensory loss in the C6 and C7 dermatomes. Electrodiagnostic studies performed 4 weeks after the injury show preserved sensory nerve action potentials (SNAPs) in these distributions. This finding is characteristic of:
items.e: In pre-ganglionic lesions (root avulsions), the dorsal root ganglion remains intact and connected to the peripheral nerve; therefore, Wallerian degeneration does not occur in the sensory axons, and SNAPs remain preserved despite clinical anaesthesia.
items.note: The electrophysiological distinction between pre- and post-ganglionic lesions is a classic exam topic and is correctly represented.

items.q: A 24-year-old male presents with a flail, anaesthetic arm after a high-speed motorcycle accident. Nerve conduction studies performed at 4 weeks demonstrate preserved Sensory Nerve Action Potentials (SNAPs) in the median and ulnar distributions despite complete clinical anaesthesia. This finding is most indicative of:
items.e: In preganglionic root avulsions (proximal to the dorsal root ganglion), the cell bodies remain intact and connected to the peripheral axon. Therefore, the SNAP remains preserved even though the patient has no sensation because the sensory signal cannot reach the spinal cord.
items.note: The question correctly tests the physiological distinction between pre- and postganglionic lesions using SNAPs, which is a classic exam topic.

items.q: In the surgical management of an adult with an upper trunk brachial plexus injury, the 'Oberlin transfer' is a widely used technique to restore elbow flexion. This procedure involves the transfer of:
o: Spinal accessory nerve to the suprascapular nerve
A fascicle of the ulnar nerve to the biceps motor branch
A fascicle of the median nerve to the brachialis motor branch
Intercostal nerves to the musculocutaneous nerve
items.e: The Oberlin transfer specifically refers to the transfer of a fascicle of the ulnar nerve to the motor branch of the biceps. The 'double fascicular transfer' (Mackinnon) adds a median nerve fascicle to the brachialis branch.
items.note: The eponym and specific nerve fascicles involved are accurately described and are high-yield for superspeciality exams.

items.q: Which clinical finding in a newborn with obstetric brachial plexus palsy is considered the most critical prognostic indicator for poor spontaneous recovery, often necessitating microsurgical exploration between 3 and 9 months of age?
o: Absence of biceps recovery (elbow flexion) by 3 months
Isolated wrist drop with intact shoulder abduction
Presence of a positive Tinel sign in the neck
items.e: According to the Gilbert and Tassin criteria, the recovery of the biceps (elbow flexion) by 3 months is the classic prognostic indicator. Absence of biceps function at this stage suggests poor spontaneous recovery and is an indication to consider surgery.
items.note: The 3-month biceps rule is the standard teaching in Campbell's and pediatric orthopaedics for OBPP management.

items.q: A patient with a suspected brachial plexus injury undergoes clinical examination. Winging of the scapula is noted, and there is clear weakness of the rhomboids (tested by hand-on-hip retraction). These findings localise the lesion to which level of the plexus?
items.e: The dorsal scapular nerve (supplying rhomboids) and the long thoracic nerve (supplying serratus anterior) both arise directly from the roots (C5 and C5-7 respectively). Paralysis of these muscles indicates a very proximal (preganglionic) root-level injury.
items.note: This tests anatomical localization based on proximal nerve branches, which is essential for distinguishing preganglionic from postganglionic injuries.

items.q: In a patient with a permanent pan-plexus injury and a flail shoulder, shoulder arthrodesis is planned to provide a stable platform. What is the recommended 'salute' position for the fusion?
items.e: The recommended position for shoulder arthrodesis in a flail arm (salute position) is approximately 20-30 degrees of abduction, 20-30 degrees of flexion, and 40 degrees of internal rotation to allow the hand to reach the mouth.
items.note: The specific angles for shoulder arthrodesis are standard orthopaedic facts frequently tested in entrance exams.

items.q: All of the following are clinical or radiographic features typically associated with a preganglionic (root avulsion) brachial plexus injury EXCEPT:
o: Presence of a pseudomeningocele on CT myelography
A positive Tinel sign in the supraclavicular area
items.e: A Tinel sign in the neck is characteristic of a postganglionic lesion (where regenerating axons are present in a neuroma). It is absent in preganglionic avulsions because the lesion is proximal to the dorsal root ganglion and no regeneration occurs distally.
items.note: The question effectively differentiates pre- and postganglionic features, which is the core of brachial plexus clinical assessment.

items.q: A 5-year-old child with a history of Erb's palsy presents with a severe internal rotation contracture of the shoulder. MRI reveals glenoid retroversion and the formation of a pseudoglenoid. This secondary deformity is best classified using the:
items.e: The Waters classification (Types I-VII) is used to describe the severity of glenohumeral dysplasia, including glenoid retroversion and posterior humeral head subluxation, which are common sequelae of obstetric brachial plexus palsy.
items.note: Waters classification is the specific eponym for glenoid dysplasia in this context, making it a high-level, appropriate question.

items.q: A 32-year-old patient presents with the sudden onset of excruciating shoulder pain that woke him from sleep. Two weeks later, the pain subsides, but he develops weakness in the serratus anterior and deltoid muscles. High-resolution ultrasound shows 'hourglass constrictions' of the affected nerve fascicles. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.e: Parsonage-Turner syndrome (neuralgic amyotrophy) typically presents with sudden severe pain followed by patchy weakness as the pain resolves. Hourglass constrictions of the nerve fascicles on ultrasound or MRI are a pathognomonic finding.
items.note: The clinical presentation and the specific imaging finding (hourglass constrictions) are pathognomonic for Parsonage-Turner syndrome.

items.q: A 24-year-old male presents with persistent pain in the anatomical snuffbox after a fall on an outstretched hand two weeks ago. Initial radiographs were reported as normal. What is the most cost-effective and sensitive next step to confirm an occult scaphoid fracture and avoid unnecessary prolonged immobilization?
o: CT scan along the long axis of the scaphoid
items.e: MRI is the gold standard for occult scaphoid fractures with sensitivity and specificity near 100%. Early MRI is considered cost-effective as it allows for immediate diagnosis and prevents unnecessary casting in patients without a fracture.

items.q: Regarding the blood supply of the scaphoid bone, which statement is correct based on the Gelberman anatomical studies?
o: The proximal pole receives its primary supply from the superficial palmar branch of the radial artery.
The dorsal carpal branch enters the scaphoid at the tubercle.
Approximately 70-80% of the scaphoid, including the proximal pole, is supplied via retrograde flow.
The scaphoid is 50% covered by articular cartilage, allowing multiple vascular entry points.
items.e: The dorsal carpal branch of the radial artery enters the dorsal ridge at the waist and supplies 70-80% of the bone, including the proximal pole, via retrograde flow. This explains why proximal pole fractures have the highest risk of AVN.

items.q: A 30-year-old laborer sustains a displaced scaphoid waist fracture. Which of the following radiographic parameters is a recognized criterion for instability requiring operative fixation?
o: Lateral intrascaphoid angle greater than 45 degrees
items.e: Instability criteria for scaphoid fractures include displacement >1 mm, a lateral intrascaphoid angle >45 degrees (humpback deformity), a radiolunate angle >15 degrees (DISI), or a height-to-length ratio of 0.65 or more.

items.q: The SWIFFT trial (2020) compared surgical fixation versus cast immobilization for undisplaced or minimally displaced scaphoid waist fractures. What was the primary conclusion regarding functional outcomes at one year?
o: Surgical fixation resulted in significantly better DASH scores.
Casting with early fixation of only those that progressed to non-union was as effective as primary surgery.
Surgical fixation significantly reduced the rate of secondary osteoarthritis.
Casting was associated with a 50% non-union rate in undisplaced fractures.
items.e: The SWIFFT trial found no significant difference in function (DASH scores) or pain at 1 year between primary surgery and cast immobilization (with early fixation of non-unions) for undisplaced/minimally displaced waist fractures.

items.q: A patient with a chronic scaphoid non-union and a significant humpback deformity requires reconstruction. There is no evidence of carpal arthritis. Which procedure is most appropriate to restore scaphoid length and alignment?
items.e: For a scaphoid non-union with a humpback deformity (but without AVN), a volar wedge (Fisk-Fernandez) corticocancellous graft is used to correct the flexion deformity and restore scaphoid anatomy.

items.q: In the Mayfield classification of progressive perilunar instability, Stage II is characterized by the capitate displacing dorsally relative to the lunate. This occurs through which anatomical weak point?
items.e: Mayfield Stage II involves capitolunate dislocation. The capitate escapes dorsally through the Space of Poirier, which is a weak area between the radioscaphocapitate and long radiolunate ligaments.

items.q: A 45-year-old patient presents with chronic wrist pain. Radiographs show a Stage III Scaphoid Non-union Advanced Collapse (SNAC). Which of the following statements regarding the arthritic pattern is true?
o: The radiolunate joint is involved with significant joint space narrowing.
Arthritis is limited only to the radial styloid and distal scaphoid fragment.
The capitolunate (midcarpal) joint is affected, but the radiolunate joint is spared.
Total wrist arthrodesis is the only surgical option for Stage III.
items.e: In both SNAC and SLAC wrists, the radiolunate joint is typically spared because it is spherical and congruent. Stage III involves the capitolunate (midcarpal) joint. Because the radiolunate joint is spared, motion-preserving salvage procedures like four-corner fusion are possible.

items.q: During wrist arthroscopy for a suspected scapholunate ligament tear, the surgeon observes that a 2.7 mm arthroscope can be passed through the gap between the scaphoid and the lunate. According to the Geissler classification, this is:
items.e: Geissler Grade IV represents gross instability where there is a 'drive-through sign,' meaning a 2.7 mm arthroscope can pass easily through the scapholunate or lunotriquetral interval.

items.q: A child has complete fusion of the middle and ring fingers, including side-to-side bony fusion of their distal phalanges. How is this syndactyly classified?
items.e: Bony fusion between digits makes syndactyly complex, and extension to the fingertip makes it complete. Complicated syndactyly refers to abnormal bone patterns, such as those associated with Apert syndrome or synpolydactyly.
items.note: The stem clearly establishes both complex and complete syndactyly.

items.q: During syndactyly release, which operative principle best reduces the risk of vascular compromise?
o: Release both sides of the same finger in one operation
Release only one side of a digit at a time
Use a split-thickness graft to avoid donor-site morbidity
Place the web commissure at the fingertip
items.e: Only one side of a digit should be released at a time; simultaneous release on both sides risks vascular compromise. Syndactylised digits commonly need full-thickness skin grafts because they share skin.
items.note: The stated staging principle directly addresses the risk in the stem.

items.q: Which complication is most commonly seen after surgical release of syndactyly?
items.e: Web creep, or distal migration of the reconstructed web, is the commonest complication. It is particularly associated with split-thickness grafts and early surgery.
items.note: The tested complication and its ranking are explicitly stated in the notes.

items.q: A newborn has a rudimentary, pedunculated postaxial digit attached by a narrow skin stalk. Which statement best describes this anomaly and its management?
o: Temtamy–McKusick type A; excision with collateral ligament reconstruction at 9–12 months
Temtamy–McKusick type B; ligation or surgical excision
Wassel type IV; excision of the radial thumb at about 12 months
Central polydactyly; reconstruction is usually deferred until school age
items.e: A rudimentary pedunculated postaxial digit is type B. It may be treated by nursery suture ligation, which can leave a residual bump or neuroma, or by surgical excision.
items.note: The description identifies type B, and the listed management is appropriate.

items.q: In the Swanson classification of congenital hand differences, syndactyly is classified under:
items.e: Syndactyly is a failure of differentiation, specifically failure of separation. In the same Swanson group are conditions such as camptodactyly, clinodactyly, arthrogryposis and synostosis.
items.note: The classification is unambiguous and directly supported by the notes.

items.q: Failure of apoptosis in the interdigital tissue during digit separation most directly results in which congenital hand anomaly?
items.e: Interdigital tissue is normally removed by apoptosis, with bone morphogenetic proteins involved in this process, around weeks 6–8. Failure of separation results in syndactyly.
items.note: The embryological mechanism and outcome are stated in the notes.

items.q: A 58-year-old has a well-defined palmar cord causing a 40° MCP joint contracture of the ring finger. He wants rapid recovery and accepts that further treatment may be needed if the contracture returns. Which option best fits these preferences?
items.e: Needle fasciotomy is an office-based option suited to a well-defined palmar cord causing an MCP contracture; recovery is fast and the procedure can be repeated. Its trade-off is a higher recurrence rate than limited fasciectomy.
items.note: Clear single-best answer consistent with the stated preferences and the reference notes.

items.q: A patient with Dupuytren disease has a painful palmar nodule but no cord or joint contracture. Which statement best describes management?
o: Nodule excision is indicated to prevent contracture
Limited fasciectomy is indicated because any nodule predicts progression
A steroid injection may be used for the painful nodule; a nodule alone is not an indication for surgery
items.e: A nodule without contracture is not, by itself, an indication for surgery unless it is painful. Steroid injection can be used for a painful nodule, whereas splinting alone is ineffective.
items.note: Accurate management statement with one defensible answer.

items.q: Which structure is characteristically incorporated into the Dupuytren spiral cord, placing the digital neurovascular bundle at risk during fasciectomy?
o: Transverse fibres of the palmar aponeurosis
items.e: The spiral cord includes the Grayson ligament and displaces the neurovascular bundle centrally, superficially and proximally. Cleland ligaments are dorsal to the bundle and are not involved.
items.note: The tested anatomy and surgical risk are accurately stated.

items.q: A 46-year-old man has bilateral Dupuytren contractures, a family history of the disease, and plantar fibromatosis. Which term best describes this pattern associated with aggressive disease and recurrence?
items.e: Early onset, positive family history, bilateral disease and ectopic lesions such as Ledderhose disease are features of Dupuytren diathesis, which is associated with aggressive disease and recurrence.
items.note: The clinical pattern and eponym are correctly matched.

items.q: In rheumatoid arthritis, a patient develops attritional rupture of the flexor pollicis longus over a volar scaphoid spur. What is the name of this lesion?
items.e: Mannerfelt lesion refers to attritional rupture of the flexor pollicis longus over a volar scaphoid spur. Vaughan-Jackson lesions involve sequential attritional rupture of extensor tendons.
items.note: The lesion is correctly identified and distinguished from the principal competing eponym.

items.q: A patient with rheumatoid arthritis has extensor tendon ruptures beginning at the little finger and progressing to adjacent ulnar-sided digits. Which mechanism and site are most characteristic?
o: Attrition over a volar scaphoid spur within the carpal tunnel
Attrition over the distal ulna at the distal radioulnar joint
Rupture at the flexor pulley of the ring finger
Attrition over a radial styloid spur
items.e: Vaughan-Jackson syndrome is sequential attritional rupture of the extensor tendons, typically beginning ulnarly as they pass over the distal ulna at the distal radioulnar joint.
items.note: The characteristic sequence, mechanism and site are accurately described.

items.q: When several rheumatoid upper-limb joints require surgery, which sequence is generally preferred?
o: Finger reconstruction, then wrist stabilisation, then proximal joints
Wrist stabilisation, then proximal joints, then finger reconstruction
Proximal joints first, then wrist stabilisation, then hand and finger reconstruction
The most deformed finger first, regardless of proximal joint disease
items.e: When multiple rheumatoid upper-limb procedures are planned, proximal joints are generally addressed before distal joints so the hand can be positioned in space; wrist stabilisation precedes finger reconstruction. The original stem implied that the wrist must precede proximal joints, which conflicts with the stated sequence.
items.note: Corrected the stem and distractors to test the proximal-to-distal sequence without contradicting the explanation.

items.q: A 17-year-old with a painful, congruent hallux valgus has an increased distal metatarsal articular angle. Which operative principle best avoids creating an incongruent first MTP joint?
o: Correct the DMAA with a biplanar chevron or an extra-articular osteotomy
Excise the lateral sesamoid and tighten the medial capsule
items.e: In a congruent deformity, correction by soft-tissue release alone can make the joint incongruent. A DMAA-correcting biplanar chevron or extra-articular osteotomy addresses the articular alignment.
items.note: The stem and keyed principle match the reference notes.

items.q: During a chevron osteotomy with lateral soft-tissue release, which measure helps reduce the risk of avascular necrosis of the first metatarsal head?
o: Extend the dorsolateral dissection to improve exposure
Preserve the dorsolateral and plantar-lateral soft-tissue attachments
Translate the metatarsal head by more than half its width
items.e: The metatarsal head receives important blood supply through vessels entering dorsolaterally and plantar-laterally. Excessive dorsolateral dissection, particularly with lateral release, can jeopardise that supply.
items.note: Correctly tests the vascular-risk principle for chevron osteotomy with lateral release.

items.q: A patient develops transfer metatarsalgia after hallux valgus correction. Radiographs show elevation of the first metatarsal following a diaphyseal Z-shaped osteotomy. Which complication mechanism best explains the symptoms?
o: Troughing of the Scarf fragments with loss of first-ray height
Lateral displacement of the sesamoids caused by crista erosion
Excessive correction of the hallux valgus angle
Medial migration of the abductor hallucis
items.e: Troughing during a Scarf osteotomy allows the fragments to telescope, elevating the metatarsal head and reducing its load-bearing contribution. Dorsal malunion can likewise cause transfer metatarsalgia.
items.note: The osteotomy, radiographic finding, and complication mechanism are correctly linked.

items.q: Which statement about the McBride procedure for hallux valgus is correct?
o: The original procedure includes lateral sesamoid excision, which can cause hallux varus
The modified procedure adds routine lateral sesamoid excision
Medial eminence excision alone is a reliable definitive correction
The procedure corrects first TMT hypermobility by arthrodesis
items.e: The original McBride procedure included excision of the lateral sesamoid, adductor tenotomy and medial capsulorrhaphy; sesamoid excision risks hallux varus. The modified procedure uses lateral release without sesamoid excision.
items.note: The distinction between original and modified McBride is accurate and unambiguous.

items.q: A patient has hallux valgus with a positive clinical test for first TMT hypermobility. Which radiographic finding is consistent with this assessment and may support a Lapidus procedure?
o: Dorsal translation at the first TMT joint of about 8–10 mm or more
Distal metatarsal articular angle below 10 degrees
items.e: Dorsal translation of roughly 8–10 mm or more is used as a marker of first TMT hypermobility. A Lapidus procedure addresses the deformity by arthrodesis of that joint.
items.note: The threshold and its clinical relevance are supported by the notes.

items.q: Which sequence best describes the early pathoanatomical change in hallux valgus?
o: Lateral capsule attenuation, followed by lateral drift of the first metatarsal while the sesamoids follow it
Medial capsule and medial sesamoid ligament attenuation, followed by lateral drift of the hallux while the sesamoids remain relatively anchored
Plantar plate rupture, followed by medial drift of the hallux and sesamoids
Abductor hallucis contracture, followed by lateral migration of the sesamoids with the metatarsal head
items.e: Attenuation of the medial capsule and medial sesamoid ligament allows the hallux to drift laterally under deforming tendon forces. The sesamoids remain relatively anchored, so the metatarsal head moves medially off them.
items.note: Accurately tests the early pathoanatomical sequence and sesamoid relationship.

items.q: A 52-year-old woman has progressive medial ankle pain and a flexible flatfoot. During single-limb heel rise, the heel fails to invert. Which examination finding is most sensitive for tibialis posterior dysfunction?
o: Inability to perform a single-limb heel rise or invert the heel during it
Reduced calcaneal pitch on a standing lateral radiograph
Pain on palpation of the sinus tarsi
items.e: Failure to perform a single-limb heel rise, particularly without heel inversion, is the most sensitive clinical test for tibialis posterior dysfunction. The too-many-toes sign reflects forefoot abduction but is not the most sensitive test.
items.note: Single best answer; stem, options and explanation are supported.

items.q: A patient has flexible progressive collapsing foot deformity with marked forefoot abduction and talonavicular uncoverage exceeding 40%. Which procedure most directly addresses the abduction component?
o: Lateral column lengthening by Evans osteotomy
items.e: Lateral column lengthening, usually by an Evans osteotomy, is used to correct substantial forefoot abduction with excessive talonavicular uncoverage. A common complication is lateral column overload causing lateral foot pain.
items.note: Appropriate indication and a defensible single best answer.

items.q: Which structure is the primary dynamic stabiliser of the medial longitudinal arch and the strongest invertor of the foot?
items.e: The tibialis posterior is the strongest invertor and the primary dynamic stabiliser of the medial longitudinal arch. It also helps lock the transverse tarsal joint for push-off.
items.note: Accurate, focused, and has one clearly correct option.

items.q: A patient with progressive collapsing foot deformity has a rigid hindfoot valgus and a fixed flatfoot. There is no ankle valgus. In the modified Johnson–Strom classification, which stage best fits this presentation?
items.e: Stage III is characterised by a rigid flatfoot with fixed hindfoot valgus and a ruptured or degenerated tibialis posterior tendon. Triple arthrodesis is a typical surgical treatment.
items.note: Classification and clinical description align; the absence of ankle valgus distinguishes stage III from stage IV.

items.q: A patient with flexible flatfoot has residual forefoot varus and medial column instability after hindfoot correction. Which procedure is best suited to plantarflex the medial column?
items.e: A Cotton osteotomy is a plantarflexion opening-wedge osteotomy of the medial cuneiform, used for residual forefoot varus or medial column instability. First tarsometatarsal arthrodesis is another option when indicated.
items.note: Procedure matches the stated deformity and has a single best answer.

items.q: Which statement about adult acquired flatfoot, now termed progressive collapsing foot deformity, is correct?
o: It is a purely sagittal-plane deformity centred on the talonavicular joint.
Spring ligament failure is recognised as a central contributor, and tibialis posterior dysfunction may be secondary.
Ankle valgus is an obligatory feature from the earliest stage.
Peroneus brevis is the primary dynamic stabiliser of the medial arch.
items.e: Progressive collapsing foot deformity is a complex three-dimensional deformity. Spring ligament failure is recognised as central in many cases, while tibialis posterior failure may be secondary.
items.note: Correct statement is supported; the distractors contradict the described deformity and anatomy.

items.q: A patient with flexible flatfoot undergoes lateral column lengthening. Which is the most common complication of this procedure?
o: Lateral column overload with lateral foot pain
Tibial nerve palsy from tarsal tunnel compression
items.e: Lateral column overload causing lateral foot pain is the commonest complication of lateral column lengthening. Other recognised complications include calcaneocuboid arthritis, sural nerve injury and nonunion.
items.note: The complication is correctly attributed to lateral column lengthening; the other options are not its commonest complication.

items.q: A 38-year-old man sustains an Achilles tendon rupture while pushing off with his knee extended. Plantarflexion is weak but still present. Which examination finding is the most reliable for confirming the diagnosis?
o: Loss of resting plantarflexion with the knee flexed
items.e: The Simmonds–Thompson calf-squeeze test is the most reliable clinical test: absent plantarflexion indicates rupture. Plantarflexion may remain because other tendons can still act on the foot.
items.note: Clear single-best answer and consistent with the reference notes.

items.q: During a percutaneous Achilles repair, a lateral incision is made approximately 10 cm proximal to the calcaneal insertion. Which structure is particularly at risk?
items.e: The sural nerve crosses from medial to lateral and lies lateral to the Achilles tendon about 10 cm proximal to its insertion, making it vulnerable during lateral approaches and percutaneous repair.
items.note: Anatomical relationship and operative risk are accurately stated.

items.q: A 46-year-old patient presents nine weeks after an Achilles rupture. Exploration reveals a 4 cm gap with scar tissue. According to the Kuwada classification, which category and reconstruction strategy best fit this injury?
o: Type III; V-Y advancement or tendon graft
Type IV; tendon transfer plus graft
items.e: A 3–6 cm gap is Kuwada type III, for which V-Y advancement, gastrocnemius recession, or tendon grafting may be used. Type II has a gap under 3 cm, whereas type IV exceeds 6 cm.
items.note: The chronic presentation, gap measurement, classification and matching strategy are consistent with the notes.

items.q: Which statement about rehabilitation after an acute Achilles tendon rupture managed non-operatively is correct?
o: Begin in neutral and permit passive dorsiflexion stretching during the first six weeks
Use 20–30° of plantarflexion with heel wedges, allow early protected weight bearing, and avoid passive dorsiflexion stretching for 12 weeks
Keep the ankle in maximal plantarflexion without weight bearing for 12 weeks
Use a neutral-position cast for six weeks, followed by immediate unrestricted sport
items.e: Functional treatment begins in an equinus boot, typically about 20–30° plantarflexed, with heel wedges and early protected weight bearing. Equinus is reduced gradually over 6–8 weeks, and passive dorsiflexion stretching is avoided for 12 weeks.
items.note: The stated protocol matches the reference notes; the distractors contradict functional rehabilitation principles.

items.q: A patient with chronic Achilles degeneration undergoes debridement that leaves less than half of the tendon intact. Which tendon transfer is commonly used to augment the reconstruction?
items.e: FHL transfer is commonly used when more than 50% of the Achilles tendon has been debrided. It is a strong, in-phase transfer with an adjacent vascularised muscle belly; the original stem’s wording, “less than half ... intact,” is ambiguous because it does not explicitly state the proportion debrided.
items.note: The intended answer is supported, but the original stem ambiguously describes the amount debrided rather than stating the threshold directly.

items.q: A runner has a tender fusiform swelling 4 cm proximal to the Achilles insertion. With ankle motion, the swelling moves with the tendon and the painful area shifts. Which clinical sign is described?
items.e: A painful fusiform swelling that moves with the tendon, with the painful area shifting during ankle movement, is the painful arc sign of mid-portion Achilles tendinopathy.
items.note: The described finding specifically identifies the painful arc sign.

items.q: Which of the following is NOT a feature or treatment principle of insertional Achilles tendinopathy?
o: A calcaneal enthesophyte may be present
Eccentric loading is performed on flat ground rather than into dorsiflexion
A central tendon-splitting approach may be used for debridement and reattachment
Eccentric heel drops below step level into dorsiflexion are the preferred loading approach
items.e: For insertional disease, eccentric loading is performed on flat ground to avoid loading the tendon in dorsiflexion. Debridement with reattachment using suture anchors may be performed through a central tendon-splitting approach.
items.note: There is one clearly incorrect principle among otherwise valid features and treatments.

items.q: A patient with diabetes has a plantar ulcer beneath a metatarsal head. A sterile probe passes through the ulcer and contacts bone. In a setting where diabetic foot osteomyelitis is common, how should this finding be interpreted?
o: It has a high positive predictive value for osteomyelitis
It excludes osteomyelitis unless radiographs are abnormal
It is diagnostic only when the ulcer is ischaemic
It has no diagnostic value without a positive superficial swab
items.e: A positive probe-to-bone test has a high positive predictive value for osteomyelitis in high-prevalence settings. Superficial swab cultures are unreliable.
items.note: Accurately reflects the prevalence-dependent interpretation of the probe-to-bone test.

items.q: A patient with diabetes has a deep foot ulcer with surrounding cellulitis extending more than 2 cm. There is no systemic toxicity. Under the IWGDF/IDSA infection severity classification, this is:
items.e: Cellulitis extending over 2 cm qualifies as a moderate infection, even without systemic toxicity. Severe infection is associated with SIRS or systemic toxicity.
items.note: The stem distinguishes moderate local infection from severe systemic infection.

items.q: A neuropathic plantar ulcer is being assessed for osteomyelitis. Which imaging investigation is most sensitive and specific?
items.e: MRI is the most sensitive and specific imaging investigation for diabetic foot osteomyelitis. Confluent low T1 marrow signal is the most specific MRI finding.
items.note: MRI is the supported best imaging option for suspected diabetic foot osteomyelitis.

items.q: A patient with diabetes has a warm, dry foot and bounding pedal pulses. Which mechanism best explains these findings?
o: Autonomic neuropathy causing anhidrosis and arteriovenous shunting
Sensory neuropathy causing loss of protective sensation
Motor neuropathy causing intrinsic muscle weakness
Infrapopliteal arterial disease causing medial arterial calcification
items.e: Autonomic neuropathy causes dry skin through anhidrosis and can produce a warm foot with bounding pulses through arteriovenous shunting.
items.note: The findings are characteristic of autonomic neuropathy.

items.q: Which statement about diabetic foot ulcer classification is correct?
o: Wagner grade 3 denotes localised forefoot gangrene
Wagner grade 2 denotes a deep ulcer reaching tendon, capsule or bone without abscess or osteomyelitis
The University of Texas system uses infection severity as its depth grade
In the University of Texas system, stage A denotes an infected ulcer
items.e: Wagner grade 2 describes a deep ulcer reaching tendon, capsule or bone without abscess or osteomyelitis. The University of Texas system grades depth and stages ulcers by infection and ischaemia.
items.note: The correct Wagner grade and University of Texas distinctions are accurately tested.

items.q: A patient with a neuropathic plantar ulcer has no clinical infection or ischaemia and no deep or draining wound. Which offloading treatment is the gold standard?
items.e: A total contact cast is the gold standard for offloading neuropathic plantar ulcers because it is non-removable and encourages compliance. It is contraindicated with infection, ischaemia, or deep or draining wounds.
items.note: The stem excludes the listed contraindications to total contact casting.

items.q: A patient with a diabetic foot ulcer has a falsely high ankle–brachial index because of non-compressible arteries. Which test is an appropriate alternative for assessing limb perfusion?
items.e: Medial arterial calcification can make the ankle–brachial index falsely high. Toe pressures are an appropriate alternative; a pressure over 40 mmHg is associated with healing.
items.note: Toe pressure assesses perfusion when ankle arteries are non-compressible.

items.q: A patient with diabetes has a forefoot plantar ulcer associated with limited ankle dorsiflexion and Achilles contracture. Which procedure can reduce forefoot pressure, but may cause transfer ulceration if overlengthened?
items.e: Achilles tendon lengthening can reduce forefoot pressure and lower recurrence of forefoot plantar ulcers. Overlengthening can transfer excessive pressure to the heel and cause heel ulceration.
items.note: The procedure and its heel-ulceration risk match the clinical scenario.

items.q: A patient with recurrent ankle sprains reports that the ankle gives way on uneven ground. The anterior drawer and talar tilt tests show no pathological laxity. Which type of instability best describes this presentation?
items.e: Subjective giving way without demonstrable pathological laxity is functional instability, commonly associated with proprioceptive deficit or peroneal weakness. Mechanical instability is characterised by pathological laxity on examination.
items.note: Clear distinction between functional and mechanical instability.

items.q: A 27-year-old athlete has persistent giving way after an inversion sprain. After six months of peroneal strengthening, proprioceptive rehabilitation and bracing, symptoms continue; examination confirms lateral ligament laxity. The ATFL and CFL tissue is suitable for repair. Which operation is the standard anatomic procedure?
items.e: The modified Broström-Gould procedure is the gold-standard anatomic repair: the ATFL and CFL are imbricated or shortened, with reinforcement by the inferior extensor retinaculum. Free tendon reconstruction is generally reserved for failed repair or poor-quality tissue and other selected cases.
items.note: Appropriate indication and a single standard anatomic repair answer.

items.q: During evaluation of chronic lateral ankle instability, stress radiographs show an anterior talar translation of 11 mm on the affected side and 7 mm on the opposite side. Which interpretation is most appropriate?
o: Abnormal anterior drawer, supporting ATFL insufficiency
Normal anterior drawer because the side-to-side difference is under 5 mm
Abnormal talar tilt, supporting isolated CFL insufficiency
items.e: An anterior drawer over 10 mm in absolute terms or about 3 mm or more side-to-side is abnormal and supports mechanical lateral instability involving the ATFL. Talar tilt is the stress measure associated with CFL insufficiency.
items.note: The absolute and side-to-side measurements both support an abnormal anterior drawer.

items.q: A patient with chronic lateral ankle instability has a cavovarus hindfoot. Which additional operative principle is most likely to reduce the risk of failure of ligament stabilization?
o: Perform a peroneus brevis tenodesis in every case
Correct the cavovarus alignment when indicated
Immobilise the ankle permanently after repair
items.e: Uncorrected cavovarus alignment can contribute to failure of lateral ligament stabilization. Correction may include a lateralising calcaneal osteotomy and, when indicated, a first metatarsal dorsiflexion osteotomy.
items.note: The operative principle and examples are supported by the notes.

items.q: A patient with an acute grade III lateral ankle sprain has no associated fracture. Which initial approach is supported for improving early outcomes while avoiding prolonged immobilisation?
o: Below-knee cast for six weeks without weight bearing
Brief protection in a cast or boot for about 10 days, followed by functional rehabilitation
Immediate operative repair of the ATFL and CFL
Unrestricted sport as soon as pain permits, without rehabilitation
items.e: For most lateral sprains, functional treatment with early mobilisation and rehabilitation is favoured over immobilisation. A short period of cast or boot protection, about 10 days, can improve early outcomes in grade III injuries.
items.note: Reflects the supported short-protection approach for grade III sprains.

items.q: Which statement about the lateral ankle ligaments is correct?
o: The ATFL is extracapsular and taut in dorsiflexion
The CFL is intracapsular and crosses only the ankle joint
The PTFL is the weakest lateral ligament and is commonly injured first
The CFL is extracapsular, lies deep to the peroneal tendons and crosses the ankle and subtalar joints
items.e: The CFL is extracapsular, forms the floor of the peroneal tendon sheath and crosses both the ankle and subtalar joints. It is taut in dorsiflexion and resists inversion in neutral or dorsiflexion.
items.note: One correct anatomical statement; the other options contradict established ligament anatomy.

items.q: A patient sustains a displaced talar neck fracture with subtalar dislocation but no tibiotalar dislocation. CT confirms the subtalar joint is dislocated rather than merely subluxed. Which Hawkins subtype best describes the injury?
items.e: A displaced talar neck fracture with subtalar dislocation is Hawkins II; Vallier subdivided this into IIA for subtalar subluxation and IIB for subtalar dislocation. The IIB pattern carries the higher AVN risk within type II.
items.note: Clear, single-best-answer classification question.

items.q: After reduction of a displaced talar neck fracture-dislocation, the skin is no longer threatened but the soft-tissue envelope remains swollen. Which statement best guides the timing of definitive fixation?
o: Definitive ORIF must be performed immediately to prevent AVN
Definitive ORIF can be delayed until the soft tissues allow
A Hawkins sign must appear before ORIF is performed
The injury should be treated in a cast because delayed fixation is contraindicated
items.e: Urgent reduction of the dislocation addresses the emergency, particularly when the skin is at risk. Definitive ORIF may be delayed until the soft tissues permit; fixation timing itself does not determine AVN rates.
items.note: Accurately distinguishes urgent reduction from timing of definitive fixation.

items.q: Which radiographic view is specifically designed to provide the best assessment of the talar neck?
o: Canale view: 15° pronated with a 75° cephalad-tilted AP beam
Broden view with the foot in internal rotation
Mortise view with the ankle in maximal plantarflexion
Oblique view with the foot in 30° external rotation
items.e: The Canale view is obtained with the foot pronated 15° and the AP beam tilted 75° cephalad. It is the best radiographic view for assessing the talar neck.
items.note: Technique and tested view agree with the reference notes.

items.q: At 7 weeks after a talar neck fracture, an AP ankle radiograph shows a subchondral radiolucent band in the talar dome. What is the most appropriate interpretation?
o: It indicates talar dome collapse from AVN
It is the Hawkins sign and suggests revascularisation
It confirms a non-union of the talar neck
It is diagnostic of post-traumatic subtalar arthritis
items.e: The Hawkins sign is a subchondral lucent band in the talar dome, typically seen at 6–8 weeks, and indicates revascularisation. Its presence is a favourable prognostic sign, although its absence does not establish that AVN will occur.
items.note: Correct timing, finding, and interpretation.

items.q: A snowboarder has persistent pain just anterior and inferior to the tip of the lateral malleolus after an injury initially diagnosed as an ankle sprain. CT shows a displaced lateral process fracture measuring 1.2 cm. What is the preferred treatment?
o: Excision of the entire talar body
items.e: A large displaced lateral process fracture, particularly one over 1 cm, is treated with ORIF. CT helps identify these fractures, which can be mistaken for ankle sprains.
items.note: The fracture size and displacement support ORIF; the alternatives are inappropriate for this pattern.

items.q: A patient falls from a height and sustains a calcaneal fracture. Which fragment is considered relatively constant because it remains attached to the talus by the interosseous and deltoid ligaments?
items.e: The sustentaculum tali is the relatively constant fragment, tethered to the talus by the interosseous and deltoid ligaments. The flexor hallucis longus runs beneath it.
items.note: Tests a standard calcaneal fracture anatomy fact stated in the notes.

items.q: A patient has a displaced intra-articular calcaneal fracture with a fracture line extending from the posterior facet to the tuberosity and a fragment displaced superiorly in continuity with the Achilles attachment. Which Essex-Lopresti pattern is this?
items.e: In the Essex-Lopresti tongue-type pattern, the secondary fracture line extends posteriorly to the tuberosity, leaving a posterior fragment that includes the tuberosity. The alternative major pattern is joint-depression type.
items.note: Fracture description identifies the tongue-type pattern unambiguously.

items.q: A patient with bilateral calcaneal fractures after a fall from height reports new back pain. Which associated injury should be specifically considered?
items.e: Calcaneal fractures from axial loading are associated with lumbar spine fractures, particularly at L1. Bilateral calcaneal fractures and other lower-limb injuries may also accompany the injury.
items.note: The association with lumbar spine injury, particularly L1, is stated in the notes.

items.q: A footballer has recurrent giving-way episodes after a non-contact pivoting injury. Which examination manoeuvre is most sensitive for detecting an ACL tear?
o: Lachman test with the knee at 20–30°
Anterior drawer test with the knee at 90°
items.e: The Lachman test is the most sensitive clinical test for ACL injury and is performed with the knee flexed 20–30°. The anterior drawer may be less sensitive acutely because of hamstring guarding.
items.note: Single best answer; the distractors are distinct assessment methods.

items.q: Which ACL bundle is primarily taut in extension and contributes most to resisting rotational loads?
o: Both bundles are equally taut only at 90°
Neither bundle contributes to rotational restraint
items.e: The posterolateral bundle is tight in extension and resists rotational loads, including the pivot-shift mechanism. The anteromedial bundle is tight in flexion and is the primary restraint to anterior translation at 90°.
items.note: Bundle function and tension pattern match the reference notes.

items.q: After ACL reconstruction, a patient has loss of flexion and the graft is tight in flexion. Which technical error most likely explains this?
items.e: An excessively anterior femoral tunnel can make the graft tight in flexion, causing loss of flexion or graft stretching/failure. An excessively anterior tibial tunnel more typically causes roof impingement in extension; the original options included duplicate posterior tibial tunnel distractors.
items.note: Replaced duplicate, poorly discriminating distractors with distinct tunnel-placement errors.

items.q: Which statement about meniscal injury associated with ACL deficiency is correct?
o: Acute ACL injuries more often involve the medial meniscus; chronic deficiency more often involves the lateral meniscus.
Acute ACL injuries more often involve the lateral meniscus; chronic deficiency increases posterior-horn medial meniscal tears.
Both acute and chronic ACL deficiency predominantly cause anterior-horn medial meniscal tears.
Meniscal tears are uncommon in chronic ACL deficiency because the menisci do not restrain translation.
items.e: The lateral meniscus is more commonly torn in acute ACL injuries, often involving the posterior horn or root. With chronic ACL deficiency, the medial meniscus becomes a secondary restraint and its posterior horn is more prone to tearing.
items.note: Accurately tests the stated acute and chronic meniscal injury patterns.

items.q: A patient with an ACL tear has a displaced bucket-handle meniscal tear and a locked knee. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Continue rehabilitation until swelling has fully resolved
Delay all intervention until at least 6 months after injury
Perform isolated ACL reconstruction without addressing the meniscal tear
items.e: A locked knee from a bucket-handle tear requires urgent arthroscopy. This does not mean ACL reconstruction must automatically be performed urgently; reconstruction timing otherwise depends on recovery of swelling, full extension, and quadriceps control.
items.note: Clarifies that urgency applies to arthroscopy for the locked knee, not necessarily immediate ACL reconstruction.

items.q: Which radiographic finding is a lateral capsular avulsion from the lateral tibial plateau and is classically considered pathognomonic of an ACL tear?
items.e: A Segond fracture is an avulsion from the lateral tibial plateau involving the lateral capsule/anterolateral structures and is classically associated with ACL tear. The lateral femoral notch sign is a deep sulcus of the lateral femoral condyle, not a tibial avulsion.
items.note: Qualified the absolute pathognomonic claim while retaining the standard exam association.

items.q: Which statement about graft choice for ACL reconstruction is correct?
o: Hamstring grafts provide bone-to-bone healing in 6–8 weeks.
BPTB grafts are associated with less anterior knee pain than hamstring grafts.
Hamstring grafts smaller than 8 mm have higher revision rates.
Allografts have lower failure rates than autografts in young, active patients.
items.e: Hamstring grafts under 8 mm in diameter are associated with higher revision rates, particularly in young or female athletes. BPTB provides bone-to-bone healing but can cause anterior knee and kneeling pain; allografts fail more often in young, active patients.
items.note: One supported correct statement; the other options contradict established graft characteristics.

items.q: During arthroscopy, a radial tear is seen crossing the mid-body of the lateral meniscus. Which mechanical function is most directly compromised?
o: Conversion of axial load into circumferential hoop stress
Resistance to longitudinal splitting by radial tie fibres
items.e: A radial tear transects the dominant circumferential fibres, disrupting hoop-stress function and impairing load transmission.
items.note: Correct and unambiguous.

items.q: A 56-year-old woman reports a sudden pop while squatting, followed by medial knee pain. MRI shows extrusion of the medial meniscus measuring 4 mm and a tear close to its posterior attachment. Which statement best describes this lesion?
o: It is a horizontal cleavage tear, usually associated with a parameniscal cyst
It is a posterior root tear, functionally similar to total meniscectomy
It is a ramp lesion at the posterior medial meniscocapsular junction
It is a bucket-handle tear, suggested by a double PCL sign
items.e: A medial posterior root tear commonly presents in middle-aged women with a pop during squatting; extrusion over 3 mm supports the diagnosis. Root disruption is functionally equivalent to total meniscectomy.
items.note: Stem and answer match the characteristic root-tear presentation.

items.q: A 24-year-old athlete has a repairable vertical longitudinal tear in the posterior horn of the medial meniscus. Which repair method is regarded as the gold standard for this location?
o: Outside-in repair with horizontal mattress sutures
Inside-out repair with vertical mattress sutures
items.e: Inside-out repair is the gold-standard technique for mid-body and posterior meniscal tears, and vertical mattress sutures provide strong fixation by capturing circumferential fibres. A posteromedial approach is used to protect the saphenous nerve.
items.note: Correct technique and suture orientation for the described tear.

items.q: Which statement about meniscal vascularity in the adult is correct?
o: The inner white-white zone lies within 3 mm of the rim and has good healing potential
The red-white zone lies 3–5 mm from the rim and has moderate healing potential
The entire medial meniscus is vascular, whereas only the lateral rim is vascular
The peripheral 10–30% of both menisci is uniformly avascular
items.e: The red-white zone is approximately 3–5 mm from the rim and has moderate healing potential. The inner white-white zone is avascular, while vascularity is limited to the peripheral portion of each meniscus.
items.note: The stated zone and healing potential are correct; the other options misstate location or vascularity.

items.q: A 9-year-old has a snapping knee, and MRI demonstrates a thick, hypermobile lateral meniscus. Which Watanabe type is associated with absent posterior meniscotibial attachment and attachment only through the meniscofemoral ligament of Wrisberg?
items.e: The Wrisberg variant is Watanabe type III. It lacks the posterior meniscotibial (coronary) attachment, leaving the meniscus hypermobile and potentially causing snapping knee syndrome in children.
items.note: Correct classification; the additional type IV option is clearly not the described Wrisberg variant.

items.q: A 33-year-old with persistent pain in a meniscus-deficient compartment after meniscectomy is being assessed for meniscal allograft transplantation. Which combination best fits the usual candidate profile?
o: Age 42, Outerbridge grade II, stable knee, corrected alignment, BMI 29
Age 42, Outerbridge grade IV, stable knee, normal alignment, BMI 29
Age 42, Outerbridge grade II, uncorrected varus malalignment, stable knee, BMI 29
Age 42, Outerbridge grade II, stable knee, normal alignment, BMI 38
items.e: A typical candidate is under about 50, symptomatic after meniscectomy, has minimal arthritis (Outerbridge under III), a stable and normally aligned or corrected knee, and BMI under about 35.
items.note: Only option A meets the stated candidate criteria.

items.q: Which radiographic finding is part of the classic Fairbank changes following meniscectomy?
o: Widening of the lateral joint space
Osteochondral loose bodies in the suprapatellar pouch
items.e: Fairbank changes include femoral condyle flattening, marginal ridge (osteophyte) formation, and joint-space narrowing after meniscectomy.
items.note: Flattening of the femoral condyle is a classic Fairbank change.

items.q: A 17-year-old sustains a first-time lateral patellar dislocation. MRI shows a bone bruise on the medial patellar facet and lateral femoral condyle. This pattern most strongly indicates:
items.e: Contusions of the medial patellar facet and lateral femoral condyle are characteristic of transient lateral patellar dislocation. MRI can also identify associated osteochondral injury.
items.note: Correct, supported MRI pattern with one clear best answer.

items.q: A true lateral knee radiograph shows a trochlear floor line crossing the anterior border of the lateral femoral condyle, with a supratrochlear spur but no double contour. Which Dejour type is present?
items.e: Dejour type B combines the crossing sign with a supratrochlear spur and has a flat or convex trochlea. A double contour would indicate type C or D.
items.note: The specified radiographic signs uniquely identify Dejour type B.

items.q: A patient with recurrent lateral patellar instability has a CT TT-TG distance of 23 mm. Which interpretation is most appropriate?
o: Abnormal, consistent with lateralisation of the tibial tubercle
Normal, because the abnormal threshold is over 24 mm
Abnormal only if measured on MRI
Normal, because the usual value is about 20–25 mm
items.e: A TT-TG distance over 20 mm is abnormal and reflects lateralisation of the tibial tubercle. MRI measurements are usually about 2–4 mm smaller than CT measurements.
items.note: The threshold and interpretation are clear for the stated CT measurement.

items.q: Which statement about the medial patellofemoral ligament (MPFL) is correct?
o: It is the primary restraint to lateral translation from 0° to 30° of flexion
It is the main restraint beyond 30° of flexion
It attaches to the distal third of the medial patellar border
It is rarely injured in first-time patellar dislocation
items.e: The MPFL provides about 50–60% of restraint to lateral patellar translation between 0° and 30° of flexion. Trochlear geometry becomes the main restraint beyond about 30°.
items.note: The tested role and flexion range are directly supported by the notes.

items.q: A 16-year-old with open physes has a first-time lateral patellar dislocation. Imaging shows trochlear dysplasia and patella alta, without a loose body. Which factor most supports considering surgery even after this first dislocation?
o: The combination of young age, dysplasia, patella alta and open physes
A normal patellar height with isolated medial retinacular tenderness
A single episode of apprehension on examination
items.e: Young patients with open physes who also have dysplasia and patella alta have a high recurrence risk, reported at over 50–70%. These features can support surgery after the first dislocation.
items.note: The high-risk combination is supported; the stem appropriately asks what supports considering, not mandates, surgery.

items.q: During reconstruction for recurrent patellar instability, which graft fixation approach best reflects the standard technique described in the notes?
o: Fix the graft at the anatomic Schöttle point with the patella centred, at about 30–60° of flexion, avoiding excessive tension
Fix the graft distal to the adductor tubercle with the knee in full extension and maximal tension
Fix the graft at the tibial tubercle with the knee at 90° of flexion
Fix the graft to the medial patellar border with the knee in full flexion and maximal tension
items.e: MPFL reconstruction uses femoral fixation at the anatomic Schöttle point, with the patella centred in the trochlea and the graft fixed at about 30–60° of flexion. Over-tensioning should be avoided.
items.note: The correct option matches the stated technique; the alternatives specify non-anatomic fixation or inappropriate tension and position.

items.q: A 19-year-old contact-sport athlete has a first traumatic anterior shoulder dislocation. After reduction, he asks about recurrence and whether early stabilisation is reasonable. Which statement is most accurate?
o: Recurrence is uncommon below age 20, so surgery is generally avoided
Recurrence may approach 70–90%; selective primary arthroscopic stabilisation can substantially reduce it in young contact athletes
Recurrence is determined mainly by the direction of immobilisation, and an external-rotation sling consistently prevents it
Recurrence is approximately 10–15%, similar to that in patients over 40
items.e: Recurrence after a first dislocation is strongly related to age and is about 70–90% in patients under 20. In young contact or collision athletes, primary arthroscopic stabilisation may be offered selectively and reduces recurrence.
items.note: Accurate age-related recurrence estimate and appropriately qualified surgical option.

items.q: A patient with recurrent anterior shoulder instability undergoes MRI. The inferior glenohumeral ligament is avulsed from the humerus and assumes a J-shaped appearance. What is the most appropriate interpretation?
o: ALPSA lesion; mobilise the medially displaced labrum before repair
HAGL lesion; repair may be open or arthroscopic
Perthes lesion; the labrum is avulsed with intact periosteum
GLAD lesion; the labral tear is accompanied by articular cartilage injury
