items.e: A J-shaped inferior glenohumeral ligament on MRI is characteristic of a humeral avulsion of the glenohumeral ligament (HAGL). If missed, it can cause recurrent instability; repair can be open or arthroscopic.
items.note: The imaging sign and lesion description match HAGL; the distractors are distinct labral lesions.

items.q: A patient has recurrent anterior instability with 12% glenoid bone loss. The Hill-Sachs interval is greater than the calculated glenoid track. Which treatment best addresses this pattern?
items.e: A Hill-Sachs interval greater than the glenoid track defines an off-track lesion, which has a high recurrence risk after isolated Bankart repair. With glenoid bone loss below 25%, the described algorithm pairs Bankart repair with remplissage.
items.note: The off-track lesion and sub-25% glenoid bone loss fit the stated treatment algorithm.

items.q: Which statement about the static stabilisers of the glenohumeral joint is correct?
o: The superior glenohumeral ligament is the principal restraint to anterior translation at 90° abduction and external rotation
The posterior band of the inferior glenohumeral ligament resists posterior translation in flexion and internal rotation
The middle glenohumeral ligament is the most important restraint in the apprehension position
The anterior band of the inferior glenohumeral ligament chiefly resists inferior translation in adduction
items.e: The posterior band of the inferior glenohumeral ligament resists posterior translation when the shoulder is flexed and internally rotated. The anterior band is the key restraint to anterior translation in abduction and external rotation.
items.note: Correctly identifies the posterior IGHL band’s restraint and position.

items.q: A 68-year-old presents with persistent shoulder weakness after reduction of an anterior dislocation. Which investigation is most appropriate to assess the likely associated injury?
o: Ultrasound or MRI of the rotator cuff
3D CT en face view of the glenoid
MRI assessment for a J-shaped inferior glenohumeral ligament
items.e: In an older patient, persistent weakness after reduction should raise suspicion of a rotator cuff tear. Ultrasound or MRI can assess the cuff, and early repair is recommended when a tear is identified.
items.note: The age and persistent weakness point to a cuff tear; ultrasound or MRI assesses it.

items.q: Which pattern is classified as Stanmore Polar III shoulder instability?
o: Traumatic structural instability associated with a Bankart lesion
Atraumatic structural instability associated with capsular laxity or dysplasia
Instability caused by abnormal muscle recruitment without a structural lesion
Multidirectional instability treated surgically with a Bankart repair
items.e: Polar III represents non-structural instability due to abnormal muscle patterning. Physiotherapy and biofeedback are used, while surgery should be avoided.
items.note: Polar III describes muscle-patterning instability without a structural lesion.

items.q: A 68-year-old has a degenerative full-thickness rotator cuff tear with active forward elevation of 70° but full passive elevation. Which description best fits this finding?
items.e: Pseudoparalysis is active forward elevation below 90° despite full passive range of motion and is associated with massive cuff tears.
items.note: Correct definition; single clear answer.

items.q: A thrower has shoulder pain in abduction and external rotation. Imaging shows an articular-sided partial tear of the posterior supraspinatus with a posterosuperior labral lesion. Which mechanism best explains this combination?
o: Subacromial impingement from a hooked acromion
Internal impingement against the posterosuperior glenoid
Medial subluxation of the long head of the biceps
Compression of the cuff in the critical zone
items.e: Internal impingement occurs when the posterosuperior glenoid contacts the undersurface of the posterior supraspinatus and anterior infraspinatus in abduction and external rotation; it is associated with articular-sided partial tears and posterosuperior labral lesions.
items.note: Mechanism and associated lesions are correctly described.

items.q: In the Ellman classification of partial-thickness rotator cuff tears, a tear measuring 4 mm in depth is:
items.e: Ellman grade 2 denotes a tear 3–6 mm deep. Grade 1 is under 3 mm, while grade 3 is over 6 mm and represents more than 50% tendon thickness.
items.note: The measurement falls unambiguously within grade 2.

items.q: A chronic full-thickness tear is retracted to the level of the glenoid. Which Patte stage describes this retraction?
items.e: Patte stage 3 indicates retraction to the glenoid. Stage 1 is close to the insertion and stage 2 is at the humeral head.
items.note: The described landmark corresponds directly to stage 3.

items.q: During examination, a patient can keep the arm in external rotation with it at the side, but has marked weakness of external rotation when the arm is abducted to 90°. Which muscle is most specifically implicated?
items.e: Teres minor contributes to external rotation in abduction and is tested with Hornblower’s sign. Infraspinatus is the principal cuff muscle for external rotation with the arm at the side.
items.note: The position-specific action distinguishes teres minor from infraspinatus.

items.q: A patient with shoulder pain has a subscapularis tear and medial subluxation of the long head of the biceps. Which structure normally helps stabilise the biceps in the bicipital groove?
o: Biceps pulley formed by the superior glenohumeral and coracohumeral ligaments
Rotator cable between the supraspinatus and teres minor
items.e: The long head of the biceps is stabilised at the groove by the biceps pulley, which includes the superior glenohumeral and coracohumeral ligaments, as well as the transverse humeral ligament. Subscapularis tears are associated with medial biceps subluxation.
items.note: The option identifies the relevant pulley components; the explanation appropriately notes the additional transverse humeral ligament.

items.q: An active patient sustains an acute traumatic full-thickness rotator cuff tear and has good preoperative muscle quality. What is the preferred timing of repair?
o: After at least 6 months of physiotherapy
Only after radiographic cuff tear arthropathy develops
Timing does not affect the chance of retraction or fatty infiltration
items.e: Acute traumatic tears in active patients are generally repaired early, within about 3–6 weeks, before retraction and fatty infiltration progress.
items.note: Matches the stated recommendation for acute traumatic tears in active patients.

items.q: A 22-year-old footballer reports groin pain with prolonged sitting and pivoting. Internal rotation is restricted, FADIR reproduces his pain, and imaging shows cam morphology. Which combination best establishes femoroacetabular impingement syndrome?
o: Hip or groin symptoms, clinical signs, and cam or pincer morphology on imaging
A positive FADIR test without symptoms
A labral tear on MRI, regardless of symptoms or examination
items.e: The Warwick Agreement defines FAI syndrome by the triad of symptoms, clinical signs, and imaging findings. Cam or pincer morphology alone is not sufficient because it can occur in asymptomatic people.
items.note: Accurate, single-best-answer application of the Warwick Agreement.

items.q: A young male athlete has a reduced femoral head-neck offset and an alpha angle of 68° on a 45-degree Dunn view. At arthroscopy, the anterosuperior acetabular cartilage is delaminated in a wave-like pattern. Which mechanism best explains this lesion?
o: Labral crushing from linear contact due to acetabular over-coverage
Outside-in abrasion from the aspherical femoral head-neck junction
Posteroinferior contrecoup injury from the femoral head levering out
Instability caused by excessive femoral anteversion
items.e: This is cam-type impingement: the aspherical femoral head-neck junction abuts the acetabulum during flexion and internal rotation, producing outside-in chondrolabral separation and cartilage delamination.
items.note: The stem and lesion pattern correctly identify cam-type damage.

items.q: Which imaging finding is most specifically associated with acetabular retroversion on an AP pelvis radiograph?
items.e: The crossover sign, in which the anterior acetabular wall crosses the posterior wall, indicates acetabular retroversion. The other findings describe cam morphology.
items.note: The options are distinct radiographic findings, and the crossover sign is the retroversion finding.

items.q: A 27-year-old with hip pain has a lateral centre-edge angle of 18° and a labral tear. Which management principle is most appropriate?
o: Isolated arthroscopic labral debridement and capsulotomy
Periacetabular osteotomy to address the underlying dysplasia
Arthroscopic cam resection as the sole treatment
items.e: An LCEA under 20° indicates acetabular dysplasia. Periacetabular osteotomy addresses the deficient coverage; isolated arthroscopic labral debridement or capsulotomy can cause severe instability.
items.note: Correctly tests dysplasia recognition and the risk of isolated arthroscopy.

items.q: A 31-year-old has symptomatic FAI despite four months of activity modification, physiotherapy, and NSAIDs. Imaging shows preserved joint space and no significant dysplasia. Which is the best next step?
o: Offer hip arthroscopy after discussing expected benefits and risks
Proceed directly to total hip arthroplasty
Continue non-operative treatment because arthroscopy does not improve outcomes over physiotherapy
items.e: Hip arthroscopy is considered for symptomatic FAI that persists despite an adequate trial of non-operative care, when joint space is preserved. The UK FASHIoN trial found better patient-reported outcomes with arthroscopy than with best conservative care at 12 months.
items.note: The clinical scenario fits the stated indication, and the trial comparison is accurately represented.

items.q: During hip arthroscopy using a perineal post, which complication is most directly associated with the post and prolonged traction?
o: Lateral femoral cutaneous nerve injury from the anterior portal
Femoral neurovascular bundle injury from medial portal placement
Sciatic nerve injury from a posterolateral portal
items.e: Perineal-post pressure and prolonged traction can cause pudendal nerve neurapraxia, as well as perineal skin or genital injury. Limiting traction time helps reduce these risks.
items.note: Correctly distinguishes a traction-post complication from portal-related risks.

items.q: In the management of pincer-type FAI, which operative step best addresses acetabular over-coverage while preserving the labral seal?
o: Acetabular rim trimming with labral takedown and re-fixation
Femoral head-neck osteochondroplasty with labral excision
Isolated capsulotomy without treating the acetabular rim
Labral debridement followed by further acetabular rim resection
items.e: Pincer morphology is treated with acetabuloplasty; the labrum may be taken down and re-fixed. Excessive rim resection risks iatrogenic under-coverage.
items.note: Correct operative principle with a clear warning against over-resection.

items.q: During the late cocking and early acceleration phases of throwing, approximately 64 Nm of valgus torque is generated at the elbow, exceeding the tensile strength of the UCL. Which structures help resist the remaining load?
o: Biceps tendon, annular ligament and radial collateral ligament
Flexor-pronator mass, radiocapitellar joint and posteromedial olecranon
Triceps tendon, anterior capsule and coronoid process
Common extensor origin, radial head and posterior capsule
items.e: The valgus load exceeds the UCL’s ultimate tensile strength, so the flexor-pronator mass, radiocapitellar articulation and posteromedial olecranon provide additional resistance.
items.note: Accurate, supported biomechanics with one defensible answer.

items.q: A 20-year-old pitcher has medial elbow pain during late cocking and early acceleration. With the elbow flexed, the examiner applies valgus stress and rapidly extends it; pain is reproduced between 70° and 120°. Which test is being performed?
items.e: The moving valgus stress test reproduces UCL-related pain in the 70°–120° shear-angle range and is highly sensitive for UCL injury.
items.note: The manoeuvre and pain arc identify the moving valgus stress test.

items.q: An MR arthrogram in a throwing athlete shows contrast tracking distally along the ulna from the undersurface of the UCL at its distal attachment. What is this finding called?
items.e: The T sign describes contrast tracking distally along the ulna beneath the UCL, indicating a partial tear at the sublime tubercle.
items.note: The described distal undersurface contrast tracking is the T sign.

items.q: A young competitive thrower has a symptomatic proximal UCL avulsion, good-quality ligament tissue and no chronic attenuation. Which procedure is an appropriate option that may allow a faster return to play than reconstruction?
o: UCL reconstruction using a palmaris longus graft
UCL repair augmented with suture tape
Arthroscopic excision of the medial epicondyle
items.e: Repair with internal brace augmentation is an option for selected proximal or distal avulsions with good tissue quality in young athletes and is associated with faster return than reconstruction. Reconstruction is used for many chronic or poor-quality tears and generally has a longer return-to-play timeline.
items.note: Changed the absolute claim of faster return to the supported qualified comparison.

items.q: A 15-year-old gymnast has lateral elbow pain and restricted motion. Imaging shows an unstable focal subchondral lesion of the anterolateral capitellum that involves more than half its width. Which treatment is most appropriate?
o: Rest from throwing for 3–6 months alone
Osteochondral autograft transfer from the knee
Observation for spontaneous reossification of the whole capitellar nucleus
items.e: A large capitellar OCD lesion, particularly one exceeding about 50% of the width or involving the lateral margin, is an indication to consider osteochondral autograft transfer. Microfracture is used for smaller lesions.
items.note: The unstable, large focal OCD lesion supports OATS.

items.q: Which statement about the UCL bundles is correct?
o: The transverse bundle is the primary restraint to valgus stress at 90°
The posterior bundle is the primary valgus restraint from 20° to 120°
The anterior bundle is the primary valgus restraint from about 20° to 120°
The anterior and transverse bundles have no stabilising role
items.e: The anterior bundle is the principal restraint to valgus stress through approximately 20°–120° of elbow flexion. The transverse bundle, or Cooper ligament, has no stabilising role.
items.note: The tested bundle function is correctly stated and the alternatives are clearly false.

items.q: A thrower has posterior elbow pain at ball release and loss of terminal extension. Repeated forced extension with valgus stress reproduces posteromedial pain, and radiographs show a posteromedial olecranon osteophyte. During arthroscopic treatment, which principle should guide resection?
o: Resect the entire posteromedial olecranon to prevent recurrence
Excise the osteophyte while preserving the normal olecranon, and assess the UCL
Resect the radial head to reduce lateral compression
Avoid osteophyte excision and reconstruct the UCL in every case
items.e: The osteophyte should be excised without over-resecting normal olecranon, because excessive resection increases UCL strain. UCL insufficiency can coexist with valgus extension overload and should be assessed.
items.note: Accurately tests the resection principle and need to assess the UCL.

items.q: A 24-year-old sprinter develops sudden posterior thigh pain while accelerating. MRI shows a partial injury at the musculotendinous junction of the biceps femoris long head. Which feature best explains the common site and mechanism of this injury?
o: A single-joint muscle injured during concentric contraction
A two-joint muscle injured during eccentric contraction
A muscle belly injured during isometric contraction
A tendon insertion injured during passive stretching
items.e: Muscle strains commonly occur at the myotendinous junction of two-joint muscles during eccentric contraction. The biceps femoris long head is the commonest hamstring muscle injured.
items.note: Accurate, supported, and has one clear best answer.

items.q: A footballer sustains a complete proximal avulsion of all three hamstring tendons during forced hip flexion with the knee extended. He is active and presents 2 weeks after injury. What is the preferred management?
o: Surgical repair, preferably within about 4–6 weeks
Immobilisation for 6 months before considering surgery
Surgical repair only if sciatic nerve palsy develops
items.e: Complete avulsion of all three proximal hamstring tendons in an active patient is an indication for surgical repair. Early repair, generally within about 4–6 weeks, gives better outcomes; the sciatic nerve lies nearby.
items.note: The injury pattern and timing are supported by the notes.

items.q: A 19-year-old basketball player has focal shin pain. Initial radiographs are normal, but MRI demonstrates a stress injury of the anterior cortex of the mid-tibia with a persistent transverse lucency. Which description and management consideration are most appropriate?
o: Low-risk compression-side injury; relative rest is usually sufficient
High-risk tension-side injury; delayed healing may require intramedullary nailing
Medial tibial stress syndrome; the lucency is a typical periosteal finding
Insufficiency fracture; unrestricted weight-bearing is recommended
items.e: The anterior mid-tibial cortical lesion, often called the dreaded black line, is a high-risk tension-side stress fracture, particularly seen in jumping athletes. It may fail to heal and can require intramedullary nailing.
items.note: Correctly identifies a high-risk anterior tibial stress fracture and its management consideration.

items.q: A 22-year-old ballet dancer has progressively worsening midfoot pain after a rapid increase in training. Radiographs are unremarkable. Which combination is most appropriate for suspected navicular stress injury?
o: CT for assessment; non-weight-bearing cast for 6–8 weeks or screw fixation in an athlete
Bone scan for definitive grading; immediate unrestricted weight-bearing
Ultrasound; corticosteroid injection followed by early return to dance
Repeat radiographs in 48 hours; relative rest only because the injury is low risk
items.e: The navicular is a high-risk stress-fracture site, with the central third vulnerable because of its blood supply. CT is used for assessment; treatment may involve 6–8 weeks of non-weight-bearing casting or screw fixation in athletes.
items.note: Supported imaging and treatment options with a single best answer.

items.q: An athlete reports predictable lower-leg pain and occasional foot numbness during running. Symptoms settle after stopping. Which investigation is used to confirm chronic exertional compartment syndrome?
o: Compartment pressure measurement before and after exercise
items.e: Chronic exertional compartment syndrome is confirmed with compartment pressure testing. Commonly used Pedowitz thresholds are at least 15 mmHg before exercise, 30 mmHg at 1 minute after exercise, or 20 mmHg at 5 minutes after exercise.
items.note: The confirmatory investigation and stated thresholds match the reference notes.

items.q: Which statement about the female athlete triad and relative energy deficiency in sport (RED-S) is correct?
o: The triad is limited to athletes with a diagnosed eating disorder
RED-S applies only to female athletes and primarily affects bone
The triad comprises low energy availability, menstrual dysfunction and low bone mineral density
Combined oral contraceptives restore bone mineral density by correcting low energy availability
items.e: The female athlete triad consists of low energy availability, menstrual dysfunction and low bone mineral density, with each feature existing on a spectrum. RED-S is a broader IOC concept that can affect both sexes and multiple body systems; oral contraceptives do not restore BMD.
items.note: Accurate distinction between the triad and broader RED-S; the alternatives are contradicted by the notes.

items.q: A distance runner develops Achilles tendon pain after starting ciprofloxacin while also taking corticosteroids. Which drug-related complication is most directly associated with this combination?
items.e: Fluoroquinolones such as ciprofloxacin are associated with tendinopathy and tendon rupture, particularly involving the Achilles tendon. Risk is increased in older patients, with corticosteroid use and with renal impairment.
items.note: Clear, supported drug–tendon association.

items.q: A 2-month-old infant has a shallow but stable hip on ultrasound, with a Graf alpha angle of 54°. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Repeat ultrasound in 6 weeks to 3 months
items.e: In an infant under 3 months, a Graf IIa hip with an alpha angle of 50–59° represents physiological immaturity. Repeat ultrasound in 6 weeks to 3 months is recommended.

items.q: During examination of a newborn, adduction and posterior pressure on a flexed hip produces a palpable sensation that the femoral head is dislocating. Which test is being performed?
items.e: The Barlow test applies adduction and posterior pressure to assess whether a hip is dislocatable. Ortolani uses abduction and elevation of the greater trochanter to reduce a dislocated hip.

items.q: A 5-month-old infant is being evaluated for suspected DDH. Which imaging investigation is most appropriate at this age, before the femoral head ossific nucleus is visible?
o: AP pelvis radiograph using Hilgenreiner and Perkin lines
items.e: Ultrasound is used up to about 4–6 months, before the femoral head ossific nucleus appears, and Graf assessment uses a static coronal view. The stem is internally inconsistent: at 5 months the ossific nucleus may already be visible, so the age alone does not establish that ultrasound is preferred; it has been clarified to specify that it is not visible.

items.q: A 7-month-old with DDH undergoes closed reduction and is placed in a hip spica cast. Which investigation is preferred to confirm that the hip remains reduced?
o: Repeat dynamic ultrasound as the sole confirmation
items.e: MRI is preferred for confirming reduction after reduction in a spica cast because it does not use radiation. CT is another option.

items.q: An infant treated in a Pavlik harness develops quadriceps weakness. The hips have been held in excessive flexion. What is the most likely complication and appropriate response?
o: Femoral nerve palsy; stop or adjust the harness
Brachial plexus palsy; increase hip flexion
Avascular necrosis; tighten the posterior straps
Posterior acetabular wall erosion; force further abduction
items.e: Excessive hip flexion, particularly beyond 120°, can cause femoral nerve palsy with quadriceps weakness. The harness should be stopped or adjusted.

items.q: A dislocated hip remains unreduced after 4 weeks in a Pavlik harness. Which management decision is most appropriate?
o: Continue the harness for several more months
Abandon the Pavlik harness and proceed to another reduction strategy
Tighten the posterior straps to force abduction
items.e: If the hip has not reduced within 3–4 weeks, the Pavlik harness should be abandoned. Prolonged use with a persistently dislocated head risks posterior acetabular wall erosion, termed Pavlik harness disease.

items.q: In a walking child with bilateral DDH, which combination of clinical features is characteristic?
o: Trendelenburg gait with apparent shortening on Galeazzi testing
Asymmetric skin folds with a positive Barlow test
Limited abduction only when the hips are extended
items.e: Bilateral DDH in a walking child can produce a waddling gait and hyperlordosis. The original stem asked for the most characteristic combination, but that wording implies a unique ranking not established by the notes; the revised stem asks which combination is characteristic. Galeazzi testing is negative in bilateral DDH.

items.q: Which combination correctly describes the normal Graf ultrasound angles of the hip?
o: Alpha angle at least 60°; beta angle under 55°
Alpha angle under 43°; beta angle over 77°
items.e: A mature Graf type I hip has an alpha angle of at least 60° and a beta angle under 55°. The alpha angle reflects the bony roof, while the beta angle reflects the cartilaginous roof.

items.q: A 7-year-old boy has a painless limp and restricted hip abduction. Radiographs show a small, sclerotic femoral ossific nucleus and a subchondral crescent. Which Waldenström stage is represented?
items.e: The initial stage features a smaller, sclerotic ossific nucleus and may show a subchondral fracture (crescent sign). Fragmentation follows and is the stage of greatest mechanical vulnerability.
items.note: The findings and keyed stage are accurate, and the alternatives are distinct Waldenström stages.

items.q: At what point should the Herring lateral pillar classification be assessed for prognostic use in Perthes disease?
o: At the initial stage, before sclerosis develops
At the start of the fragmentation stage
items.e: Herring classification is assessed at the start of fragmentation. It grades the height of the lateral 15–30% of the femoral epiphysis on the AP radiograph.
items.note: The timing and description of the lateral pillar are correct and yield one defensible answer.

items.q: A 9-year-old with Perthes disease has a lateral pillar B pattern. Which management statement is most accurate?
o: Observation is preferred because children under 10 do not benefit from containment
Surgical containment may give better results than non-operative treatment
A lateral pillar B pattern has a poor outcome regardless of treatment
Bracing is proven to prevent femoral-head deformation
items.e: For children over 8 years with lateral pillar B or B/C disease, surgical containment can produce better results than non-operative treatment. Containment aims to keep the head within the acetabulum during fragmentation.
items.note: The age and lateral-pillar category fit the stated containment indication; the distractors contradict the supplied evidence.

items.q: A child with Perthes disease has restricted abduction, and arthrography shows that the extruded femoral head hinges on the lateral acetabular edge during abduction. Which procedure is a salvage option for this mechanical problem?
items.e: This describes hinge abduction, in which the head is not containable and hinges on the lateral acetabular edge. A valgus (extension) osteotomy can bring the congruent part of the head into the weight-bearing zone.
items.note: The described mechanics and salvage procedure match; the main competing osteotomy is for containment.

items.q: Which radiographic finding is the earliest sign of Perthes disease?
o: Flat femoral head with a flat acetabulum
items.e: The crescent sign represents a subchondral fracture and is the earliest radiographic sign. Lateral calcification and metaphyseal cysts are head-at-risk signs, while a flat head is a later shape outcome.
items.note: The keyed finding and the distinctions from risk signs and late deformity are supported.

items.q: A boy presents with knee pain and a limp. On the AP pelvis radiograph, a line drawn along the superior femoral neck fails to intersect the lateral femoral epiphysis. This line is:
items.e: Klein's line is drawn along the superior border of the femoral neck and normally intersects the lateral femoral epiphysis. Failure to do so supports the diagnosis of SCFE.
items.note: This is the standard description of Klein's line in SCFE.

items.q: A 3-year-old has irregular ossification of the femoral head, with similar findings on the other side. The process is expected to resolve spontaneously. Which diagnosis best fits?
items.e: Meyer dysplasia typically causes irregular femoral-head ossification in children under 4 years, is often bilateral, and resolves spontaneously. The original 5-year-old age lies outside the typical age in the reference notes.
items.note: Corrected the age to fit the characteristic Meyer dysplasia presentation stated in the notes.

items.q: A newborn has a flexible forefoot adduction deformity with a normal hindfoot and ankle. The forefoot is fully correctable by passive abduction. What is the most appropriate management?
items.e: A fully passively correctable positional deformity can be managed with stretching. Serial casting and clubfoot surgery are not indicated for this flexible deformity with a normal hindfoot and ankle.
items.note: The marked answer, reassurance and observation, does not match the supplied reference note, which specifies stretching only.

items.q: During Ponseti correction of idiopathic clubfoot, where should counter-pressure be applied while abducting the supinated foot?
items.e: The lateral talar head is the fulcrum for abduction. Pressure at the calcaneocuboid joint can lock the calcaneus and prevent it from rotating beneath the talus.
items.note: Correct and supported; the options are distinct fulcrum or pressure sites.

items.q: A 4-month-old infant with clubfoot has undergone serial casting. The foot is abducted to 65°, but ankle dorsiflexion remains 5°. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Begin dorsiflexion before correcting the remaining deformity
Percutaneous Achilles tenotomy followed by a final cast
Apply a short-leg cast for three weeks
items.e: If dorsiflexion remains under about 10–15° after adequate abduction, percutaneous Achilles tenotomy is indicated. The final cast is applied after tenotomy.
items.note: The sequence and threshold match the supplied notes; the marked next step is the single best answer.

items.q: Which finding contributes to the hindfoot contracture score in the Pirani assessment of clubfoot?
items.e: The hindfoot score includes the posterior crease, empty heel and rigid equinus. The other listed findings belong to the midfoot score.
items.note: Correctly distinguishes the hindfoot and midfoot components of the Pirani score.

items.q: A child who previously completed Ponseti treatment returns with dynamic supination while walking on the lateral border of the foot. The child is 3 years old, the deformity is flexible, and the lateral cuneiform is ossified. Which procedure is most appropriate?
o: Tibialis anterior tendon transfer to the lateral cuneiform
items.e: Dynamic supination from an overactive tibialis anterior in an appropriately aged child with a flexible foot is treated with tendon transfer to the lateral cuneiform.
items.note: The clinical features match the stated indication for tendon transfer.

items.q: Which statement about the foot abduction orthosis used after Ponseti correction is correct?
o: Both feet are positioned in 60–70° of external rotation
The affected foot is positioned in about 60–70° of external rotation and the normal foot in about 30–40°
The bar is set narrower than shoulder width
It is worn only at night for the first three months
items.e: The affected foot is set at about 60–70° external rotation and the normal foot at about 30–40°, with a shoulder-width bar. The brace is worn for 23 hours daily for three months before transitioning to nights and naps.
items.note: The correct position and bracing schedule are accurately stated in the notes.

items.q: Which external fixation system, an Indian contribution, is used for gradual correction of neglected or recurrent clubfoot in older children?
items.e: Joshi's external stabilisation system (JESS) is an external fixation method used for gradual correction of neglected or recurrent clubfoot in older children. The other options are osteotomy or fusion procedures, not external fixation systems.
items.note: The original stem implies failure of non-operative treatment, but its answer identifies a method for gradual correction; asking directly about the system makes the tested fact precise.

items.q: A 6-year-old has an extension-type supracondylar fracture. After reduction, the hand is warm and pink but no radial pulse is palpable; perfusion remains satisfactory. What is the best next step?
o: Immediate anterior exploration of the brachial artery
Admit, elevate the limb and monitor perfusion closely
Repeat closed reduction and insert a medial pin
Discharge after pinning with routine follow-up
items.e: A perfused pink pulseless hand after reduction can be observed closely in hospital. Exploration is indicated if perfusion deteriorates or if a median nerve palsy is associated.
items.note: Matches the recommended management of a pink pulseless hand.

items.q: During fixation of a displaced paediatric supracondylar humerus fracture, which pin configuration provides stable fixation for most fractures while avoiding the nerve risk associated with a medial pin?
o: Two or three divergent lateral pins, separated at the fracture site
Two parallel lateral pins entering close together at the fracture site
One lateral pin and one medial pin placed with the elbow hyperflexed
Two crossed pins inserted percutaneously without extending the elbow
items.e: Two or three divergent lateral pins with separation at the fracture site are stable for most fractures and avoid the ulnar nerve risk of a medial pin. If a medial pin is needed, a small incision and elbow extension help protect the nerve.
items.note: Correct lateral-pin configuration and nerve-risk comparison.

items.q: A 9-year-old has an apparently sprained ankle after an inversion injury. The distal fibular physis is tender, but radiographs show no definite fracture. Which injury should be suspected?
o: Salter-Harris I fracture of the distal fibula
Salter-Harris II fracture of the distal fibula
Salter-Harris III fracture of the distal fibula
Salter-Harris V fracture of the distal fibula
items.e: In children, the physis is weaker than the surrounding ligaments, so an apparent sprain may be a physeal injury. A Salter-Harris I distal fibular injury can have normal radiographs, although physeal widening may be visible.
items.note: Classic presentation of a potentially occult distal fibular SH-I injury.

items.q: Which statement about growth disturbance after physeal injury is correct?
o: A physeal bar involving 60% of the physis is generally treated by bar resection if growth remains
A bar involving under 50% of the physis may be resected with interposition when at least 2 years of growth remain
Park-Harris lines converging on the physis indicate symmetrical growth
Salter-Harris V injuries have the most favourable growth prognosis
items.e: Bar mapping is performed with MRI or CT. Resection with interposition is considered when the bar involves under 50% of the physis and at least 2 years of growth remain; converging Park-Harris lines suggest a bar.
items.note: The stated bar size and remaining-growth criteria are correct.

items.q: A child’s elbow radiograph shows an ossified fragment within the joint, but the trochlear ossification centre is not yet visible. Which diagnosis best explains this finding?
items.e: The medial epicondyle ossifies before the trochlea. An ossified fragment in the joint before the trochlear centre appears is therefore an incarcerated medial epicondyle.
items.note: Uses the established order of elbow ossification centres.

items.q: After reduction of a supracondylar humerus fracture, the Baumann angle differs from the opposite elbow by 7°. What does this most strongly indicate?
o: A normal variation that cannot reflect reduction quality
A sagittal-plane deformity measured by the anterior humeral line
items.e: A change in Baumann angle exceeding 5° compared with the opposite side indicates coronal malalignment. The anterior humeral line is used to assess sagittal alignment.
items.note: The threshold and plane assessed by the Baumann angle are correct.
